The statistical tests used are reported in different sections of the methodology and not always in a systematic manner, making it challenging to obtain a comprehensive view of the analyses performed. We therefore recommend including a more structured and concise section that clearly summarizes all the applied tests, the type of data analysed, and the rationale behind the choice of each statistical test. Alternatively, we suggest including a subsection on the statistics and software used within each section of the methodology. This will allow the reader to better understand the different statistical approaches used. 2. Assumptions behind the use of parametric tests When parametric tests were used instead of non-parametric ones, it is not specified whether the assumption of normality of the data distribution was verified. An example of this is the use of the paired t-test to evaluate the IUA score. Since this is a score, it is likely that nonparametric tests would be more appropriate. Or, if a parametric test is needed, it would be appropriate to state the rationale for such a choice. 3. Choice of statistical test for organoid quantification A two-way ANOVA test was used in the organoid quantification section. It would be useful for the authors to clarify the rationale for using a two-way analysis. A two-way ANOVA analyses the effect of two different categorical independent variables on a continuous dependent variable. It is not clear what the two independent variables are in this case. In addition, it is important to specify whether there were two independent interacting factors. Could it be that a one-way ANOVA would have been more appropriate? 4. Statistical power and sample size calculation The authors calculated the sample size based on a hypothetical increase in live births from 0% to 28%. The hypothesis is probably correct. However, this sample size calculation assumes that the primary objective of the trial is to examine the percentage of women who have a pregnancy that ends in a live birth. For all the other analyses that have been performed, namely those related to secondary and exploratory endpoints, this sample calculation is not as crucial. To give just one example, when it comes to endometrial volume or thickness a sample calculation based on the proportion of life births has no reason to be (even if it is still a paired cohort study). It is sufficient to say that a convenience sample was studied, or the sample size should be computed on a hypothetical difference on volumes or thickness. In any case, in the description of the sample size calculation, the authors do not report the statistical power value used for the estimate. It is recommended that the power and alpha values assumed in the calculation are explicitly reported. 5. Typographical errors. Finally, we suggest a review of, e.g. in the methods section: “Patients were managed as described previously described…”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_6: General This phase 1/2 trial assessed the safety, efficacy, and biological plausibility of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy for treating moderate to severe Asherman Syndrome (AS) in 20 infertile women unresponsive to prior treatments. The therapy was well-tolerated, with reversible limb paresthesia as the most common side effect. Significant improvements were observed in endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. Clinically, menstruation and reproductive function were restored, leading to six live births following embryo transfer. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed partial reversion of AS-related changes, and mitochondrial variant tracking showed insights into stem cell engraftment. The results suggest this therapy is safe and effective, warranting further investigation in larger trials. The manuscript is well-written, grammatically sound, and addresses a highly interesting topic, combining stem cell applications as orphan drugs with single-cell technologies. However, some technical aspects related to the bioinformatics analyses, such as the use of older packages (CellRanger, Seurat), as well as the provision of analysis scripts, could benefit from refinement. Major 1. How was the concentration of mobilized cells (at least 30 million cells with >70% purity and >50% viability) determined for this study? Is this concentration commonly used for CD133+ BMDSCs in this application? In cardiac regeneration studies, similar cell collections often use lower concentrations, how does this compare to your approach? 2. Could you explain the rationale behind using CellRanger Software version 3.1.0 (from July 2019) for this analysis, given that the current version is 9.0.1? Additionally, I noticed that Seurat version 4 was used, whereas version 5 is available for quite some time. The use of these older versions, both for CellRanger and Seurat, can potentially result in different analysis outcomes due to improvements or changes in data processing and downstream analysis methods introduced in newer versions. 3. Did the authors also perform quality assessments using tools like MultiQC to aggregate the overall quality of the samples? It might be beneficial to provide these quality reports as supplemental material to account for the sequencing quality. 4. Did the authors also perform dataset integration using Harmony (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0619-0) in addition to the SCT transformation, which is commonly considered a standard approach for handling batch effects, particularly when samples have been processed in different batches? While Harmony is mentioned in the methods section, it appears to be described within the machine learning part, rather than in the single-cell processing section. Could you clarify when Harmony was applied in the analysis and why it was not used in all experiments? 5. Could you please include the cell-to-cell communication analyses in the methods section? 6. Providing the relevant scripts in a public repository would greatly enhance the overall reproducibility and depths of the data analysis. Minor 1. The required number of patients is inconsistent between the methods section and the study protocol, 20 versus 22. It may be helpful for the authors and readers to standardize and use a single number throughout the entire work. 2. The authors also may provide the exact version of the genome build used GRCh38-3.0.0. 3. Did the authors used specific databases, tools or scientific literature to annotate the single cell clusters - Reference 3 in the main manuscript (results) might be added also in the methods section in more detail, if the annotation is mainly based on previous works of the authors, including the species under investigation (e.g., murine, cell-based, …). 4. How was the selection of the 9 out of 20 patients was conducted for the single-cell analysis? 5. Please remove the “.” In the middle of the sentence in line 327.

peer_review_rounds.author_response: Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): Review of the article by Santamaria et al “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial’.The authors are reporting a non-randomized prospective open label trial on autologous hematopoetic stem cell therapy for Asherman syndrome cases resistant to existing therapies. The group has been working on the possibility of such therapy for over a decade now, and while this approach is cumbersome, expensive and possibly not available for many, it is an important pathophysiology driven treatment that has a potential. I want to commend on use of lineage tracing experiments showing the engra ftment of the CD133+ cells, and on demonstrated changes in the cell populations by single-cell RNA seq studies. Please see comments below. Comments: 1. Line 114, “the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse event…”. What do you mean? You mean this was the most serious adverse event? It was only in 1 patient, and what about chest pain or bleeding? A1. Thank you for your comment. Indeed, the term “treatment-emergent adverse effect” may seem confusing, and we have modified it “adverse event”. In the same manner, we have noticed that we mentioned limb paresthesia, which was a common effect before stem cell instillation, but the AEs we report here occur after administration. We have now modified the wording and now we refer to the most frequent AE after apheresis, which was nausea, headache and arm pain. We have included it in the text as indeed this was not clear in the current text (see line 118: “The most common adverse events after stem cell administration included arm pain, headache and nauseas, which in all cases were mild and reversible. Arm pain was mostly related to catheterism and was solved with local ice administration”(see table 2). 2. I suggest adding “infection” to the causes of AS. A2. We agree with the reviewer, infection has been added as a possible cause of AS (line 63): “…or after miscarriage and/or infection that disrupts the endometrial niche…”. 3. I recommend presenting the data on menstrual pattern and its recovery (before and after the treatment) in the text clearer and in Table 1 (or separately). It is an important clinical information. Provide reference for menstrual pictogram. A3. Menstrual pattern and its recovery are important clinical indicators. Since the majority of patients presented with amenorrhea or minimal bleeding at baseline, consistent with severe Asherman’s Syndrome, pre-treatment menstrual bleeding data were not recorded. This made unfeasible to apply a menstrual pictogram prior to treatment. Additionally, in accordance with the study protocol, menstrual patterns were prospectively assessed after patient enrollment. Specifically, they were assessed through 6 consecutive months following treatment. This has been now clarified in line 161: “Most patients did not have their period prior to the treatment and so menstrual blood records were prospectively assessed after therapy (1-6 months), as stated per protocol”. Further, to provide a comprehensive overview of the effects of the stem cell intervention on menstrual cycles, we present menstrual pattern data after 6 months treatment in Table 3 Pictorial Blood Assessment Chart (PBAC) Determination of total menstrual blood loss. Fertil Steril 76, 125-131 (2001). The reference for this is mentioned in the text. We refer to reference: Determination of total menstrual blood loss. Fertil Steril 76, 125-131 (2001). 4. Make sure it is clear in the Abstract and text that hysteroscopy was only diagnostic, no lysis of adhesions was performed, to be able to truly evaluate the effect of the therapy. This is really not clear. A4. Thank you for the comment. We have reviewed it through the text to make sure this is clear. Also, to clarify this concept, we have added the following statement in the Abstract (line 34) and the Methods section (line 53-54): “Hysteroscopic diagnostic evaluation was used to grade the severity of Asherman's Syndrome (AS); however, no operative hysteroscopy was performed”. 5. Table 1 and text: you did not present pregnancy rates and miscarriage rates, just live births. How many transfers were performed per patient and in total to get the 6 live births? A5. We have now added two extra columns in Table 1 indicating the number of transfers and clinical outcome (live birth, miscarriage, non-pregnancy). We performed a total of 41 embryo transfers in 19 patients, resulting in an implantation rate of 31.7% per embryo transferred (13/41) resulting in 5 live births. In addition, we recorded one spontaneous pregnancy resulting in live birth from patient N11. This has been now clarified in Table 1 and the following sentence has been added in lines 169: “we performed a total of 41 embryo transfers in 19 patients, resulting in an implantation rate of 31.7% per embryo transferred (13/41)”. 6. Lines 164-166: these conclusions should be softer as clinical significance is not clear, if any. What about difference in delta from pre- to post- in these measures? A6. Thank you for your comments. The mean change (delta) from pre- to post- measures in endometrial thickness was 1.49 +/- 0.63mm, and for endometrial volume was 1.52 +/0.80cm3 —both statistically significant (p<0.01). (Supplementary Figure 1B and 1C). Nevertheless, we have softened the conclusion and it’s included from line 184 to191: “These findings suggest that achieving an endometrial thickness of approximately 5.46 ± 0.89 mm and an endometrial volume of around 3.62 ± 0.85 cm³ may be associated with improved live birth outcomes in this study Although we show a potential association between enhanced endometrial characteristics and improved reproductive outcomes, it is important to note that live birth outcomes are also influenced by embryo transfer–related factors, such as embryo quality, number of transfers, timing, etc. These elements likely interact to determine overall success and need to be taken into consideration. 7. Line 182: what do you mean by uterine curettage was performed by operative hysteroscopy? Do you want to say that retained products of conception were removed hysteroscopically? I do hope that uterine curettage was not performed in this AS patient. A7. The reviewer is correct. We meant that the retained products of conception were removed hysteroscopically. The sentence has been revised as follows: “One of the participants experienced a first-trimester miscarriage that required hysteroscopic removal of the retained products of conception” (lines 203). 8. Single-cell RNA seq results: why would AS-epithelial cells increase after cell therapy? Aren’t they being replaced more by epithelial cells? A8. Thank you for your insightful question. We believe you are referring to Figure 4B. To clarify, in Figure 4A the cluster corresponding to AS-epithelial cells is reduced post-treatment, and Figure 4C shows that the relative abundance (cell ratio) of AS-epithelial cells decreases significantly after CD133⁺ BMDSC therapy. However, Figure 4B presents a different type of analysis: it shows the enrichment score of a gene set signature associated with endometrial functionality during the secretory phase (including genes such as SCGB1D2, MT1F, MT1X, CXCL14, WNT5A, etc.). This gene set was derived from our previous work identifying markers enriched in the early- and mid-secretory phases. Therefore, the increase observed in Figure 4B for the AS-epithelial population does not reflect a numerical increase in cell count, but rather an upregulation of this functional gene set within the remaining AS-epithelial cells post-treatment. In other words, although the proportion of AS-epithelial cells decreases (Figures 4A and 4C), those that persist exhibit higher expression of genes associated with a receptive, functional endometrium. This suggests that CD133⁺ BMDSC therapy not only shifts the cellular composition but may also reprogram the remaining AS-epithelial cells to a more functional state, contributing to improved endometrial receptivity. 9. Analysis of unique mtDNA: why only 2 patients? Also, in the text you mention only 2 patient samples, but in Figure 4E and figure legend its 3 patients, unless I am getting it wrong. A9. We apologize for the confusion. We indeed performed three of them, so the figure legend is correct (n = 3). We have now updated the text accordingly (line 295: “Comprehensive profiling in three patients revealed 32, 9 and 2 shared mtDNA variants in the endometrium post-treatment respectively…”). As of why only three patients, the MAESTER protocol needs to start with the reamplification of the left over cDNA used to run the single cell RNA seq data. In this case we only had enough good quality cDNA samples left to run MAESTER in these three samples. 10. When you get to organoids, the description of results is more chaotic and you are losing the reader. We thank the reviewer for this valuable feedback. We understand that clarity and logical flow are crucial, especially in complex sections such as the organoid experiments. To address this point, we have thoroughly revised the corresponding section of the manuscript to improve organization and readability. We believe these changes significantly improve the flow and coherence of the organoid results section and help maintain the reader’s engagement. 11. What are the in vivo controls? A11. The in vivo controls used for the organoid studies referred to endometrium obtained from healthy women that served as controls (healthy endometrium) presented in detail in our previous study by Santamaria, X., Roson, B., Perez-Moraga, R. et al., Decoding the endometrial niche of Asherman’s Syndrome at single-cell resolution, Nat Commun 14, 5890 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41656-1 12. I am not sure how you showed the improved receptivity; that’s an overstatement. A12. We think you refer to line 320, where we stated “These results may offer insights into the differences in organoid development after treatment, reinforcing the claim of glandular epithelium differentiation towards a more receptive profile after treatment”, since we do not see any claims on “improved receptivity” throughout the text. If you refer to this part, we have now modified it from line 315-318 to the following statement “Although the proportions of Post-AS therapy do not fully mirror those of healthy controls, the shift in epithelial glandular composition after treatment may indicate a trend toward functional remodeling, including an enrichment of cells with a potentially more receptive-like profile (Figure 5C)”. 13. What are the future directions? Are the authors proposing large clinical trial (RCT) or to move this therapy to clinic now, without phase 3? Not clear how this will look like. Should mention the associated health care costs and alternatives, as well as interdisciplinary approach involved in this treatment. A.13. We are currently in the process of reviewing our protocol for a Phase 3 trial from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) which will start in Q4 2025 involving approximately 30 patients. Since this condition is considered a rare disease, and we have been granted orphan drug designation by both the FDA and EMA, we are hopeful that, upon successful completion of Phase 3 and receipt of the necessary regulatory approvals, this therapy can be advanced to clinical use. Healthcare costs have not yet been calculated, as they will depend on the final approved protocol. 14. Figure 3: why didn’t you present all 19 patients that completed the treatment and post-treatment evaluations? A14. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to include additional hysteroscopy images. However, due to technical limitations at the time of patient follow-up—including temporary unavailability of the hysteroscopy equipment and, in some cases, equipment malfunction—it was not possible to systematically acquire additional endoscopic images beyond those already included in Figure 3A. Although images are not available for all patients, visualization from the side of the clinician at the time of analysis was performed, so that IUA score for all the patients is present (n=19). 15. Who was performing the hysteroscopies, before and after the treatment? Were clinicians blinded to the therapy timing such as did they know that they are doing pre- or post-stem cell therapy cavity assessment? How was their bias managed? A15. All hysteroscopies were performed by the same surgeon (XS), who was not blinded to the treatment allocation. To minimize potential bias, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) classification for intrauterine adhesions (IUAs) was strictly followed, with scoring thoroughly documented through photographic evidence and independently reviewed in a blinded manner by a second surgeon (JT). 16. When was the endometrial thickness measured, in which cycle phase? I understand that these are moderate-severe AS patients, but if you want this study to be taken seriously, you have to be consistent in when the lining thickness is measured. Where in the menstrual cycle were the 2D and 3D evaluations done, hysteroscopy and then the stem cell treatment? If amenorrhea, cycle phase could have been assessed by scanning ovaries and hormonal testing. A16. In the Methods section, under Procedures (lines 43–99) of our original paper, the reviewer can find relevant information. Specifically, during the simulated “secretory phase” (five days after progesterone administration), endometrial status was assessed both before and after treatment. This evaluation included histological digital image analysis, 2D/3D transvaginal ultrasound (Samsung, South Korea), and hysteroscopic assessment using the ASRM classification of intrauterine adhesions (IUAs)¹. Hysteroscopies were performed with a 5 mm Betocchi hysteroscope (Karl-Storz). These procedures were conducted in accordance with the protocol approved by the local ethics committee and the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS). 17. Table 1: why NA for endometrial volume assessment in 3 patients? Endometrial volume data is presented for 16 patients rather than the full cohort of 19. This discrepancy is due to a temporary unavailability of the 3D transvaginal probe, which prevented the acquisition of high-quality volumetric imaging for three patients at all required time points. Consequently, 3D imaging data could only be obtained and analyzed for 16 patients. 18. Table 2: I suggest using “false passage instead of “false path”. “Bleeding”- what is it, uterine/vaginal or intraabdominal? Vomiting (not vomit. What is Abdominal swelling, is it hives on the skin, or bloating? You should be more specific about skin rash, just localized or generalized? Also, is arm pain same as pain associated with arm hematoma? What is respiratory infection, just URI or something more serious? We have modified the wording according to the reviewer's suggestion and table 2 is now updated. 19. Was the brachial artery catheterization done under anesthesia or procedural sedation? Just with procedural sedation. This has been added in line 85 of methods doc. Minor comments: 1. Some language revision is recommended for sentence flow, and some typos and missing words. We have revised language throughout the whole text. Thank you 2. Sentence on lines 76-79: please revise, not too clear. Done. This is now line 75-77. 3. In the Results, please be consistent when writing pre-AS, pre-treatment AS or AS-pre- and -post. Both in the text and Figures. Thanks, we have consistently used pre-AS therapy and post- AS therapy throughout manuscript and figures 4. Discussion, line 306: are your references 17-23 or 28 as stated? Reference list goes to 23 only. References are 17-23, thanks, it has already been modified Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author): The authors reported the safety and efficacy of intrauterine intravascular injection of bone marrow-derived CD133+ stem cells in treating 20 cases of refractory Asherman syndrome. Single-cell sequencing of endometrial tissues from a subset of cases before and after treatment was performed to investigate the stem cell homing and differentiation，and transcriptional profile changes of the administered cells in vivo, as well as organoid formation capacity and associated expression alterations. While the study is interesting and holds significant clinical relevance, several critical aspects require further elucidation to strengthen its translational impact. 1. In the research proposal, this research was described as a prospective, multicenter, and self-controlled study. However, the current report appears to be based on work conducted at a single center. Could you please provide the reasons? A1. Thank you for the opportunity to clarify this point. As outlined in the original research proposal, the study was designed as a prospective, multicenter, self-controlled clinical trial involving three institutions: Clínica del Pilar, Vall d’Hebron, and Quirón. While all three centers contributed to specific aspects of the study, the majority of patient recruitment and data collection ultimately took place at Clínica del Pilar. This was primarily due to its stronger infrastructure and higher patient flow for the targeted clinical indication, which made it the most efficient site for enrollment. Nonetheless, the other two centers were actively involved in critical components of the protocol. Specifically: Vall d’Hebron participated in hematological assessments and catheterization procedures. Quirón was responsible for embryo transfer procedures. Clínica del Pilar conducted gynecological assessments and hysteroscopies, in addition to leading patient recruitment. Therefore, while the report may appear to reflect single-center activity due to the concentration of patient data from Clínica del Pilar, the study remains a collaborative multicenter effort, with each site contributing to different phases of the clinical workflow. 2.Result 1 On line 94, the author states that “Following diagnostic hysteroscopy, hematopoietic stem cells were mobilized, harvested through leukapheresis, and selected for CD133+ and intra-endometrial spiral arterioles instillation (Fig. 1A).” Was surgical separation of intrauterine adhesions required before injection? In which phase of the menstrual cycle should the injection be administered? A2. Hysteroscopic diagnostic evaluation was used to grade the severity of Asherman's Syndrome; however, no operative hysteroscopy was performed. Surgical separation of intrauterine adhesions was performed to facilitate endoscopic access for diagnostic evaluation. Cell injection was conducted during a simulated mid secretory phase, as all patients were receiving hormonal replacement therapy owing to the absence of spontaneous menstruation in many of them (see Methods section, lines 44-99) 3. How was the cell therapy dosage determined? Was it simply based on the amount of cells that could be isolated and obtained? A3. Thank you for your comment. In this Phase 1–2 study, the administered dose of CD133⁺ BMDSCs was not pre-specified nor determined through a dose-escalation design. Instead, it was based on the total number of CD133⁺ cells that could be isolated and enriched from each individual patient following bone marrow aspiration. The actual cell yield depended on several patient-specific factors, including their response to filgrastim, vascular access quality, and tolerance to apheresis. As a result, the observed dose range (37–166.1 × 10⁶ cells, 75% CI) reflects inter-patient variability in cell yield rather than adherence to a standardized dosing protocol. This pragmatic approach was chosen to assess the feasibility and safety of autologous cell therapy in a real-world clinical setting. 4. In secondary endpoint, I noticed that the specific location of the endometrial biopsy for comparing histological changes and immunohistochemical staining before and after treatment seems to be missing in the methodology section. Could you please provide more details on this aspect? A4. In moderate to severe Asherman syndrome, the location of endometrial biopsies depends on the presence of identifiable areas of bona fide endometrium rather than on a specific topographical site. This is detailed in the Methods section (Procedures subsection lines 55-61." Specifically, it says: Endometrial biopsies were performed under hysteroscopic vision from the posterior wall of the uterus at least 1 cm away from any visually identified IUA using a semi-rigid double-action biopsy and grasping forceps (Karl-Storz, Germany). 5. In the legend of Fig. 2, the sample sizes indicated for the box plots of endometrial volume (n=16) and endometrial thickness (n=19) appear to be inconsistent with the figure itself. It is possible that there might be a typographical error by the author. Why are the sample sizes for the analysis of endometrial thickness and endometrial volume different—one being 16 cases and the other 19 cases—when the total sample size should be 20 cases? A5. We thank the reviewer for the comment and appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point-by-point. Total cases — why not 20? Although 20 patients were initially enrolled in the study, one participant (Patient N11) voluntarily withdrew before completing the follow-up assessment and was therefore excluded from the post-treatment analysis. As a result, the total number of cases analyzed was 19. Why is the sample size for endometrial thickness 19, but 16 for endometrial volume? Endometrial thickness was measured using in situ ultrasound imaging during patient appointments. Consequently, we were able to obtain endometrial thickness data for all patients who participated in the studies (n = 19). Regarding endometrial volume, there was a period during the study when the 3D transvaginal ultrasound probe was unavailable for technical reasons. This limitation prevented us from acquiring high-quality volumetric imaging for three (12, 13 and 14) patients at all required time points. Therefore, reliable 3D endometrial volume data are available for only 16 patients. Regarding Figure 2A: Since the purpose of Figure 2A was to compare 2D and 3D measurements, we included only 16 patients for whom both endometrial thickness and volume data were available. This explains why the figure presents data for only 16 individuals. We hope this clarification resolves the reviewer’s concerns 6. Regarding the efficacy, the key efficacy endpoint is the live birth rate. From Table 1, it appears that successful pregnancy mainly depends on the severity of the disease. Could the author address this point in the manuscript? A6. Thank you for this thoughtful observation. At this stage, we believe we do not have sufficiently robust data to support a definitive conclusion regarding the relationship between disease severity and successful pregnancy outcomes. There are several limitations that preclude a meaningful analysis: Sample size: The overall number of patients included in the study is limited (n = 20), which reduces the statistical power to detect significant associations. Severity distribution: The distribution of Asherman syndrome severity among participants is imbalanced, with 12 patients classified as having moderate AS and 8 as severe. Live birth outcomes: Looking at the cases of live birth, it is true that there is a trend towards improvement in moderate cases, however, the small numbers and heterogeneity of the cohort prevent us from drawing reliable conclusions. We acknowledge the importance of this point, and we have included the following paragraph in the manuscript, specifically in lines 175-177: “Interestingly, the patients who achieved a live birth had been diagnosed with moderate-stage AS, suggesting that treatment efficacy may be influenced by disease severity. However, given the small sample size and data heterogeneity—the unequal distribution of moderate and severe cases—this observation should be considered preliminary”. 7.On line 256, the author states that “RNA-based UMAP clustering post-treatment demonstrated the presence of CD133+ mtDNA clones within diverse endometrial cell populations (Figure 4E), confirming the grafting and multilineage differentiation capacity of CD133+ BMDSC post-cell therapy.” However, it may be necessary to have experimental evidence to confirm the differentiation capacity of CD133+ BMDSC, rather than relying solely on the findings from single-cell sequencing. The viability of the cells used for treatment was >50%. Could it be that dead cells entered the body, their mitochondrial DNA was engulfed or phagocytosed by other cells, rather than differentiating into other cell types? A7. We thank the reviewer for their valuable comments. Just to clarify, as this was a Phase 1-2 clinical trial, the product specification was established in agreement with the European Medicines Agency (EMA), permitting a minimum CD133⁺ cell viability threshold of 50%. However, the actual data reported a mean of 99.7±0.27% on the cell viability for the patients, so the proposed scenario seems unlikely. We understand the 50% minimum requirement may rise some questions so to clarify this point we have now added this in methods (line 72-73) and in the draft (line 103-106) the actual results of the purity and viability of the presented patients. Regarding CD133 differentiation, we generated experimental evidence confirming the multilineage differentiation potential of CD133⁺ BMDSCs. My major points are these and further details follows below: Major points: Without a control group/placebo, interpreting the real effectiveness of the intervention is very difficult because you lack a baseline for comparison in stage 2. The main limitation of this study is that the data are limited to only one-month post-transplantation, which is not sufficient to assess the long-term safety and efficacy of the treatment. Extended follow-up, ideally up to the trial’s defined 15-month endpoint is necessary to support the conclusions. Additionally, the absence of a control group makes it difficult to confidently attribute observed effects to the treatment. While the hysteroscopic images provide some information, their value is limited due to variation in sampling location, unknown menstrual cycle phase and inconsistent hormone levels during the first month. We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed question and provide the following point-by-point response: What percentage of endometrial cells post-treatment showed donor mitochondrial DNA? We would like to highlight that our cell therapy is autologous, not allogeneic. Consequently, while mitochondrial variant tracking is a powerful tool for lineage tracing, its utility for quantifying engraftment in our setting is inherently limited, as it only detects cells carrying a mitochondrial variant (a minority of cells). In our study, only 1.12% of post-treatment endometrial cells exhibited such donor-specific mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Rather than serving as a quantitative measure of engraftment, this approach was used to characterize the phenotypic and transcriptomic identity of engrafted cells, enabling us to gain insights into their differentiation behavior within the endometrial niche. What is the most abundant cell type that bone marrow stem cells may differentiate into? Our data suggest that CD133⁺ BMDSCs most frequently differentiate into stromal and endothelial cell lineages. This interpretation is supported by transcriptomic shifts related to angiogenesis and extracellular matrix remodeling observed in scRNA-seq analyses before and after stem cell therapy. However, due to the low sample size (3 patients), these conclusions remain hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted with caution. Did engraftment correlate with clinical outcomes? While we demonstrated the presence of mitochondrial variants, it is important to note that the number of detectable variants varied between patients, and the analysis was limited to three individuals. Therefore, although we observed overall clinical improvements across the cohort—including increased endometrial volume, thickness, and live birth rates—we were unable to directly correlate mtDNA-based engraftment levels with individual clinical outcomes. Moreover, as previously stated, the autologous nature of the therapy significantly limits the ability to detect engraftment events and to establish quantitative correlations with clinical endpoints. Concerns about mtDNA transfer mechanisms (e.g., nanotubes, cell fusion, exosomes): Biologically, we believe this remains an unresolved question, as mitochondrial transfer between cells has been described, but its actual frequency and relevance in human endometrial tissue remain unclear. From a bioinformatic perspective, we acknowledge that it is not possible to definitively exclude the possibility that the mitochondrial DNA detected in recipient cells originated from transfer mechanisms. However, we applied stringent thresholds for variant calling, including only high-confidence heteroplasmic variants that were absent in pre-treatment samples and uniquely observed post-treatment, thereby strengthening the specificity of our lineage detection. Miller et al. We thank the reviewer for highlighting the relevance of the observed changes in perivascular cells and macrophages following treatment. While it is true that in the central nervous system (CNS), pericytes have been implicated in scar formation and inhibition of regeneration after injury, the role of perivascular cells in the endometrium is distinct and context-dependent. Our data demonstrate a tendency towards increase post-treatment in perivascular cells (putative pericytes), along with a marked reduction in macrophage abundance within the endometrial tissue. In contrast to the central nervous system (CNS), where pericytes have been implicated in the formation of fibrotic scar tissue that hinders regeneration after injury, pericytes in the endometrial context appear to play a distinct, pro-regenerative role. Specifically, endometrial pericytes have been associated with microvascular stability, paracrine support of angiogenesis, and interactions with endothelial and epithelial cells that contribute to cyclical regeneration of the uterine lining (Li et al., 2019). Moreover, perivascular cells in the uterus may also exhibit mesenchymal stem cell-like properties, supporting tissue repair and remodeling rather than fibrotic encapsulation (Spitzer et al., 2012). The expansion of this population post-treatment may thus reflect the activation of a regenerative niche rather than a fibrotic or inhibitory microenvironment. This is consistent with previous reports in reproductive biology suggesting that perivascular stromal cells coordinate angiogenesis and modulate immune responses during endometrial regeneration (Gargett et al., 2016). In parallel, the observed reduction in macrophage abundance—particularly those associated with inflammatory phenotypes—suggests a shift away from active inflammation toward immune resolution and tissue remodeling. This dynamic is similar to processes described in successful tissue repair across organ systems, where a timely reduction of pro-inflammatory macrophages, coupled with increased vascular support and stromal cell activation, marks a transition toward functional healing (Davies et al., 2013). These findings have now been further elaborated in the revised Discussion to clarify the functional implications of the cellular changes we observed and to distinguish the uterine regenerative context from that of CNS injury and scarring. Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): Comments on “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial” As requested by the Editor, our review will be limited to those aspects that relate to the trial design and statistics of this manuscript. We do not have sufficient experience and knowledge for evaluation of aspects that are more specific to cells and laboratory work. Considering that Asherman Syndrome has a significant impact on the quality of life of many people, and that currently the only possible intervention - which is often not definitive - is operative hysteroscopy, the identification of different approaches could be of great value. This is especially true if these possible new interventions are able to overcome infertility. Therefore, we commend the authors for their commitment to the search for new treatment options. We thus appreciated the authors’ effort in conducting this clinical trial aimed at evaluating the tolerability, safety, and efficacy of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy in patients with Asherman Syndrome (AS) refractory to surgical interventions. Overall, the methodological components of the study are appropriate for a non-randomised, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. We are of the opinion that the study design is well-structured, and we do not have any major comments on this aspect. However, considering that the study represents a complex methodological project integrating clinical and molecular approaches, we believe that some clarifications and further details may be useful, both regarding the objectives of the study and the use of statistics. This is all the more important given that the sample consisted of 20 women (one of whom did not complete the study), which is relatively large considering the prevalence of the disease, but relatively small considering the numerous endpoints set by the authors. We reiterate the importance of this study and offer some comments and suggestions to further improve the clarity, transparency and robustness of the analyses. A. We sincerely thank Reviewer #4 for the thoughtful and constructive comments, as well as the recognition of the importance of our study and the efforts made by our multidisciplinary team over the past four years. We are especially grateful for your acknowledgment of the significance of developing new therapeutic strategies for Asherman Syndrome (AS), a condition with considerable impact on patients' quality of life and limited treatment options. We appreciate your positive assessment of the trial design and the methodological framework of our non-randomized, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. Your recognition that the overall structure is appropriate and well-conceived is encouraging and greatly valued. We also acknowledge your suggestion that, given the complexity of our integrated clinical and molecular approach, additional clarifications and details regarding the study objectives and statistical analyses would enhance transparency and rigor—particularly in light of our sample size and the multiple endpoints assessed. We fully agree with this observation and have revised the manuscript accordingly to provide the following: 1. Clarified Study Objectives: We have updated the Methods section to explicitly distinguish between primary, secondary and exploratory objectives (lines 22-41) 2. Statistical Considerations: We have rewritten the statistical section part to include more details on how each analysis was performed as further described below. We hope that these revisions address your concerns and contribute to a more transparent and robust presentation of our findings. Once again, we thank you for your expert evaluation and for your helpful suggestions to improve our manuscript. Major comments 1. Partially addressed primary endpoints According to the trial registration on the European Union Clinical Trial Register (EudraCT: 2016-003975-23), three primary endpoints were declared: “1. Identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur in the patient throughout the study up until Month 15 post-treatment. 2. In the event of a term pregnancy, identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur during the pregnancy, birth and puerperal period. 3. In case of a Live Birth (LB), identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events that may be associated with the investigational medicinal product (IMP) until the first month of age.” However, in the present study, only the first primary endpoint appears to have been thoroughly developed, and its results reported. The results of the primary endpoints are reported in the manuscript on lines 109-116 and in Table 2. There is no mention of primary endpoints 2 and 3, i.e. pregnancies and births. Some information on these is provided in secondary endpoints section and in the supplementary material, but as these are primary endpoints - and therefore theoretically the most important ones - they should be clearly presented in the section of the results dealing with the primary endpoints. It would be appropriate for the authors to complete the analysis by including the remaining two primary endpoints as outlined in the registered protocol. Alternatively, the authors should state why the results of the other two primary endpoints were not reported in the primary endpoint results section and were not discussed. For example, the most outstanding result of this study is mentioned by the authors in the abstract: "...reproductive function was restored, culminating in six live births after embryo transfer". It is not clear why this striking observation is barely mentioned in the manuscript, neither in the results nor in the discussion, even if one of the primary endpoints was the “identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events” in case of a life birth. It is clear that the set of secondary and explanatory outcomes is intended to try to understand the biological and molecular reasons behind the regained fertility of some women. Nevertheless, the primary endpoint is in danger of being obscured by all the other analyses. A1. Thank you for your insightful analysis of the trial design. As noted by the reviewer, we have now provided further information of the incidence, prevalence, and frequency of various adverse events that may occur: These endpoints are now outlined in the section “primary endpoints” in lines 112-129. We have also added further explanation in the discussion (line 338-344). 2. Excessive detailing of secondary and exploratory endpoints Although the presentation of the results and discussion of the secondary and exploratory endpoints is comprehensive and thorough, the length and level of detail may be reconsidered as it seems disproportionate to the primary objectives of the study. A more concise approach could benefit the overall focus and readability of the manuscript. Alternatively, the endpoints of the study could be refocused. A2. Thank you for your comments. We have made every effort to be concise in our presentation of secondary and exploratory endpoints. However, the amount of information extracted from the exploratory (scRNA-seq) analysis to describe the molecular mechanisms of the therapy is very large and even if we have shortened it, it still requires a significant space in the manuscript. Additionally, other reviewers have requested to further emphasize into these findings, so we have had to extend certain parts of this analysis. Besides, it is important to consider the breadth of clinical, biological, and basic research that supports not only the effectiveness but also the mechanism of action of this therapy. Nonetheless, since we have now added more information about the primary end points, we believe there is now a more balanced structure between the primary and secondary/exploratory end points. 3. Predictive model based on Support Vector Machine (SVM) In the section concerning endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs), the authors add the use of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) with a kernel radial basis functon(RBF), implemented via the scPred package, to perform transcriptomic comparison with in vivo data. However, although a brief description of the process is provided (10-fold cross-validation and C parameter optimization), several key methodological elements are missing, e.g. the type of learning adopted, the target classes used for model training, the feature selection procedure, the model performance metrics, and the rationale for choosing the RBF kernel, among others. Given the complexity and methodological significance of a machine learning-based analysis, we recommend that a dedicated and detailed methods section be added. Alternatively, since this does not represent one of the study’s primary endpoints, the analysis could be considered for omission. A3. As the reviewer correctly notes, this analysis does not represent a primary endpoint of the study and may potentially confuse readers when interpreting the organoid results. Therefore, we have decided to omit it and it has been now removed from Figure 5 and methods section. Minor comments 1. Statistical methodology presentation Although the statistical methodology covers a broad range of analyses, it is overall unclear, dispersed, and difficult to follow. The statistical tests used are reported in different sections of the methodology and not always in a systematic manner, making it challenging to obtain a comprehensive view of the analyses performed. We therefore recommend including a more structured and concise section that clearly summarizes all the applied tests, the type of data analysed, and the rationale behind the choice of each statistical test. Alternatively, we suggest including a subsection on the statistics and software used within each section of the methodology. This will allow the reader to better understand the different statistical approaches used. A1. Thank you for your valuable comment. We have now structured the statistical section into various parts: Statistical analysis of clinical design and data outcomes, statistical analysis for single cell data of in vivo biopsies and statistical analysis for organoids. We believe this organization makes the statistical tests easier to access and understand. 2. Assumptions behind the use of parametric tests When parametric tests were used instead of non-parametric ones, it is not specified whether the assumption of normality of the data distribution was verified. An example of this is the use of the paired t-test to evaluate the IUA score. Since this is a score, it is likely that nonparametric tests would be more appropriate. Or, if a parametric test is needed, it would be appropriate to state the rationale for such a choice. A2. Thank you very much for this helpful comment. We have now updated the Statistical Analysis section to include the normality assessments, which had been omitted in the previous version. Specifically, we used the Shapiro–Wilk test to evaluate the normality assumption for each dataset. Regarding the use of parametric tests in Figures 2 and 3 (endometrial volume, thickness, and IUA score), we initially selected the paired t-test because the data consist of paired measurements from the same patients before and after treatment, and when normality is satisfied, parametric tests provide greater statistical power. To ensure this approach was appropriate, we tested each dataset for normality. For endometrial volume and thickness, the data met the normality assumption and thus justified the use of the paired t-test. However, for the IUA score shown in Figure 4, you are absolutely right—normality was only observed in the post-treatment data. Therefore, we additionally applied the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which yielded the same statistical significance as the paired t-test (p < 0.0001). We agree this is a more appropriate approach, and we have accordingly updated both the graph and the statistical test presented. Just to double check, we did perform now both parametric and non-parametric tests to verify robustness of results and ensure significance for both scenarios. 3. Choice of statistical test for organoid quantification A two-way ANOVA test was used in the organoid quantification section. It would be useful for the authors to clarify the rationale for using a two-way analysis. A two-way ANOVA analyses the effect of two different categorical independent variables on a continuous dependent variable. It is not clear what the two independent variables are in this case. In addition, it is important to specify whether there were two independent interacting factors. Could it be that a one-way ANOVA would have been more appropriate? A3. We employed a two-way ANOVA for organoid quantification to evaluate the effects of two independent categorical variables: (1) experimental group (AS-Pre EEO, AS-Post EEO, and Control EEO) and (2) passage number (P0, P1, P2), on the continuous dependent variable—organoid count. This analysis allowed us to assess both the main effects of group and passage, as well as their interaction, indicating whether the treatment effect varied across passages. This is particularly relevant given that organoids are cultured in a cocktail of growth factors, and repeated passaging may diminish therapeutic effects. The two-way ANOVA thus captured both group differences and passage-dependent dynamics. 4. Statistical power and sample size calculation The authors calculated the sample size based on a hypothetical increase in live births from 0% to 28%. The hypothesis is probably correct. However, this sample size calculation assumes that the primary objective of the trial is to examine the percentage of women who have a pregnancy that ends in a live birth. For all the other analyses that have been performed, namely those related to secondary and exploratory endpoints, this sample calculation is not as crucial. To give just one example, when it comes to endometrial volume or thickness a sample calculation based on the proportion of life births has no reason to be (even if it is still a paired cohort study). It is sufficient to say that a convenience sample was studied, or the sample size should be computed on a hypothetical difference on volumes or thickness. A4. Thank you for this thoughtful observation. We agree that the original sample size calculation, which was based on an expected increase in live birth rates, primarily supports the trial’s primary objective related to reproductive outcomes. For analyses related to secondary and exploratory endpoints—such as endometrial volume and thickness—we acknowledge that this calculation is not directly applicable. As suggested, we have now clarified in methods section (section Statistical analysis of clinical outcomes) that a convenience sample was used for these secondary analyses. In any case, in the description of the sample size calculation, the authors do not report the statistical power value used for the estimate. It is recommended that the power and alpha values assumed in the calculation are explicitly reported. A4. Thank you for the comment. We have now added the alpha level and statistical power to the Methods section (line 369 of the methods doc inside the subsection of “statistical analysis of clinical design”). Below are the main inputs used for the sample size calculation: • Proportion of events: Group 0 = 0.00% Group 1 = 28.00% • Minimum expected effect size: 28.00% difference • Alpha risk (Type I error): 5% • Power (1 - Type II error): 80% • Test type: One-sided • Expected dropout rate: 20% • Required sample size per group (before dropout adjustment): 18 • Adjusted sample size per group (accounting for 20% dropout): 22 5. We have amended this section, which now reads: 'Patients were managed as previously described (line 44 of methods section).' Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author): General This phase 1/2 trial assessed the safety, efficacy, and biological plausibility of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy for treating moderate to severe Asherman Syndrome (AS) in 20 infertile women unresponsive to prior treatments. The therapy was well-tolerated, with reversible limb paresthesia as the most common side effect. Significant improvements were observed in endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. Clinically, menstruation and reproductive function were restored, leading to six live births following embryo transfer. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed partial reversion of AS-related changes, and mitochondrial variant tracking showed insights into stem cell engraftment. The results suggest this therapy is safe and effective, warranting further investigation in larger trials. The manuscript is well-written, grammatically sound, and addresses a highly interesting topic, combining stem cell applications as orphan drugs with single-cell technologies. However, some technical aspects related to the bioinformatics analyses, such as the use of older packages (CellRanger, Seurat), as well as the provision of analysis scripts, could benefit from refinement. Major 1. How was the concentration of mobilized cells (at least 30 million cells with >70% purity and >50% viability) determined for this study? Is this concentration commonly used for CD133+ BMDSCs in this application? In cardiac regeneration studies, similar cell collections often use lower concentrations, how does this compare to your approach? A1. Thank you for this insightful comment. The product specification for the cell therapy—including a minimum of ≥30 million CD133⁺ cells with ≥70% purity and ≥50% viability—was established in agreement with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) during the clinical trial authorization process. As this was a Phase 1–2 trial, these criteria were designed to ensure feasibility, safety, and consistency of the product while allowing for some variability in early-stage manufacturing. Importantly, the cell dose was not arbitrarily selected but was determined by the number of CD133⁺ cells that could be realistically mobilized and recovered from each patient following G-CSF stimulation and apheresis. The threshold of 30 million cells reflected the minimum yield considered necessary for therapeutic delivery, based on preclinical work and prior experience with autologous stem cell therapies. It also accounted for the variability in mobilization capacity across patients. While some cardiac regeneration trials have used lower cell doses, the biological context and clinical indications differ significantly. Cardiac patients typically face life-threatening conditions and are often older, with reduced bone marrow stem cell mobilization capacity. In contrast, our study population comprises younger individuals who are not affected by life-threatening diseases—this is an explicit exclusion criterion of our trial.Therefore, despite administering only minimal doses of filgrastim, our patients generally exhibit higher cell yields. This enhanced mobilization capacity allows for a more robust collection of CD133+ cells. Importantly, this Phase I/II trial was designed to determine the optimal therapeutic dosage. In line with this objective—and owing to the biological advantages mentioned—it is expected that higher cell dosages will be obtained. Our primary goal was to ensure the administration of a therapeutically relevant cell dose, while simultaneously maintaining patient safety and manufacturing feasibility. 2. Could you explain the rationale behind using CellRanger Software version 3.1.0 (from July 2019) for this analysis, given that the current version is 9.0.1? Additionally, I noticed that Seurat version 4 was used, whereas version 5 is available for quite some time. The use of these older versions, both for CellRanger and Seurat, can potentially result in different analysis outcomes due to improvements or changes in data processing and downstream analysis methods introduced in newer versions. The rationale behind using CellRanger v3.1.0 (released July 2019) and Seurat v4 lies in the study’s timeline. The experimental protocol was approved and initiated on April 20, 2020, at which point CellRanger v3.1.0 and Seurat v4 were the most stable and supported versions for our pipeline. Importantly, re-analysis with newer versions would introduce inconsistencies between the original pipeline and current computational standards, potentially affecting reproducibility and interpretation. We also note that CellRanger v3.1.0 was last updated in February 2025 for archival maintenance, and Seurat v4 remained the working version throughout our analysis pipeline, even though v5 has been available since November 2023. While newer versions offer improvements, the results and conclusions of this study remain robust and directly comparable within the analytical context under which they were originally generated and published (Santamaria, X., Roson, B., Perez-Moraga, R. et al., Decoding the endometrial niche of Asherman’s Syndrome at single-cell resolution, Nat Commun 14, 5890 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41656-1) 3. Did the authors also perform quality assessments using tools like MultiQC to aggregate the overall quality of the samples? It might be beneficial to provide these quality reports as supplemental material to account for the sequencing quality. A3. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding MultiQC. Unfortunately, integrating MultiQC is not feasible in this context because the version of CellRanger (3.1.0) used in our study is not fully compatible with MultiQC’s current parsers. Therefore, we provide individual per-sample QC reports generated by CellRanger, which accurately reflect the quality of the data generated using our original pipeline. We believe this is the most appropriate approach and will include these reports as supplemental material. 4. Nat Com 2023) and the current analysis. Therefore, to maintain coherence across studies, we retained the original SCT-based integration for downstream analyses. 5. The rationale for performing stem cell treatment in mid-secretory phase is because progesterone essentially creates a “fertile ground” for the stem cells to recognize, adhere, engraft, and contribute to regeneration. Progesterone transforms the estrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory, receptive state. This includes decidualization of stromal fibroblasts, increased extracellular matrix deposition, and altered immune tolerance. Also, P4 upregulates angiogenic factors such as VEGF and angiopoietins, which make the microvasculature more permeable to circulating cells. In this primed environment, progesterone also induces expression of key chemotactic and adhesion molecules—including CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins—that are critical for guiding stem cells toward the endometrial tissue. Finally, P induces expression of factors like CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins, which guide stem cells toward the endometrial tissue (1-9). Stem cells administered via intravascular injection in uterine microcirculation can reach the spiral arterioles and venules of the endometrium. They express surface receptors such as CXCR4, which respond to progesterone-induced chemokine gradients, facilitating active homing and targeted migration into the stromal compartment. Progesterone-induced endothelial changes further support stem cell adhesion, rolling, and diapedesis into the tissue. Once engrafted, stem cells secrete growth factors (e.g., HGF, IGF-1, bFGF) that enhance epithelial proliferation, angiogenesis, and stromal repair. In some instances, mesenchymal stem cells may differentiate into endometrial stromal-like cells, replenishing damaged areas. Both progesterone and stem cells both promote a locally anti-inflammatory, pro regenerative environment, reducing fibrosis and allowing structural regeneration (10). Importantly, if stem cells were injected without progesterone priming, the endometrium may remain in a proliferative or atrophic state with lower vascular permeability, less chemokine signaling, and reduced receptivity, impairing stem cell engraftment and therapeutic efficacy. The rationale for evaluation in the mid-secretory phase is because this part of the menstrual cycle represents the most informative time point for clinical evaluation of endometrial receptivity improvements following stem cell therapy. This window allows for the assessment of key surrogate markers, including endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. These parameters provide measurable evidence of structural and functional regeneration. We understand your concern, which addresses an important methodological aspect in evaluating endometrial histology in patients with intrauterine adhesions (IUA). Geographical heterogeneity of endometrial damage is a well-recognized challenge in Asherman’s Syndrome (AS), and standardizing biopsy site selection is essential to ensure reliable interpretation of histological changes. In this study, as well as in our previous related work (Santamaria X et al., Nature Communications, 2023), biopsy site selection was deliberately standardized. Specifically, biopsies were obtained under direct hysteroscopic vision from the posterior wall of the uterus, maintaining a 1 cm margin from any visible intrauterine adhesion. This approach ensured that all samples were collected from bona fide, non-fibrotic endometrium adjacent to the pathological area—tissue most likely to reflect the therapeutic response—while maintaining consistency across timepoints. The posterior wall of the uterine cavity is among the most reproducible and accessible sampling sites, particularly in cases where extensive synechiae may limit access to other regions. Hysteroscopic guidance allowed us to avoid areas of severe fibrosis or necrosis that would preclude meaningful histological evaluation, focusing instead on viable tissue with regenerative potential. Furthermore, the literature acknowledges the existence of different adhesion types (fibrous, muscular, or mixed) that cause variable degrees of damage across the uterine cavity (Foix A et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol, 1966). Our approach accounted for this variability by consistently sampling from the perilesional functional endometrium, which is most relevant for evaluating the impact of cell therapy aimed at tissue regeneration. Specifically, it says: Endometrial biopsies were performed under hysteroscopic vision from the posterior wall of the uterus at least 1 cm away from any visually identified IUA using a semi-rigid double-action biopsy and grasping forceps (Karl-Storz, Germany)”. I have some concerns because in patients with IUA the degree of endometrial damage may not be consistent throughout the entire endometrium. Some areas may show severe fibrosis, while others may not. If we want to evaluate the effect of the cell therapy through histological changes in the endometrium, it is best to determine the sampling site of the endometrium. I am concerned that sampling the endometrium from different sites before and after therapy may affect the evaluation of the effectiveness of cell therapy. 3 In line 187, the author stated that “although we showed a potential association between enhanced endometrial characteristics and improved reproductive outcomes, it is important to note that live birth outcomes are also influenced by embryo transfer–related factors, such as embryo quality, number of transfers, timing, etc”. What dose the author mean? The author mentioned above that a single blastocyst was transferred. Could it be that the patients who failed to achieve pregnancy had poor-quality embryos? 4. One of the characteristic of this study, as the author mentioned, is that single-cell sequencing of the endometrial tissue of patients before and after cell therapy was performed, revealing changes in cell composition and gene expression. reviewer_comments.reviewer_6: Thank you very much for addressing my comments. While I understand that the use of older software versions (CellRanger 3.1.0 and Seurat 4) was specified in the original protocol from 2020, I would recommend acknowledging this limitation in the manuscript. Specifically, it would be prudent to mention that these older versions were used as per the protocol and to discuss any potential inconsistencies when compared to newer versions, which are now available. Using older software versions could potentially result in inconsistencies or missed improvements in data analysis, which may impact the comparisons with other related works in the field. Additionally, this could limit the ability of other researchers to use the provided cell annotation clusters effectively unless they also use the same older versions, which may introduce additional complications. In the rapidly evolving field of bioinformatics, keeping up with updates is generally recommended to ensure accurate and reproducible results for all researchers, especially considering that the patient data in this study cannot be stored for reanalysis in an open repository. Regarding the availability of the analysis code, I support the idea of publishing it on GitHub after acceptance. However, for a journal like Nature Communications, I believe it would be beneficial to provide the code during the revision process itself. This would allow reviewers, including myself, to verify the consistency, transparency, and reproducibility of the analysis before final publication. Once again, I appreciate your efforts in addressing these issues, and I believe the manuscript will benefit from further clarification and transparency regarding the software versions used and the availability of the analysis code.

The rationale for performing stem cell treatment in mid-secretory phase is because progesterone essentially creates a “fertile ground” for the stem cells to recognize, adhere, engraft, and contribute to regeneration. Progesterone transforms the estrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory, receptive state. This includes decidualization of stromal fibroblasts, increased extracellular matrix deposition, and altered immune tolerance. Also, P4 upregulates angiogenic factors such as VEGF and angiopoietins, which make the microvasculature more permeable to circulating cells. In this primed environment, progesterone also induces expression of key chemotactic and adhesion molecules—including CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins—that are critical for guiding stem cells toward the endometrial tissue. Finally, P induces expression of factors like CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins, which guide stem cells toward the endometrial tissue (1-9). Stem cells administered via intravascular injection in uterine microcirculation can reach the spiral arterioles and venules of the endometrium. They express surface receptors such as CXCR4, which respond to progesterone-induced chemokine gradients, facilitating active homing and targeted migration into the stromal compartment. Progesterone-induced endothelial changes further support stem cell adhesion, rolling, and diapedesis into the tissue. Once engrafted, stem cells secrete growth factors (e.g., HGF, IGF-1, bFGF) that enhance epithelial proliferation, angiogenesis, and stromal repair. In some instances, mesenchymal stem cells may differentiate into endometrial stromal-like cells, replenishing damaged areas. Both progesterone and stem cells both promote a locally anti-inflammatory, pro regenerative environment, reducing fibrosis and allowing structural regeneration (10). Importantly, if stem cells were injected without progesterone priming, the endometrium may remain in a proliferative or atrophic state with lower vascular permeability, less chemokine signaling, and reduced receptivity, impairing stem cell engraftment and therapeutic efficacy. The rationale for evaluation in the mid-secretory phase is because this part of the menstrual cycle represents the most informative time point for clinical evaluation of endometrial receptivity improvements following stem cell therapy. This window allows for the assessment of key surrogate markers, including endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. These parameters provide measurable evidence of structural and functional regeneration. We understand your concern, which addresses an important methodological aspect in evaluating endometrial histology in patients with intrauterine adhesions (IUA). In this study, as well as in our previous related work (Santamaria X et al., Nature Communications, 2023), biopsy site selection was deliberately standardized. Specifically, biopsies were obtained under direct hysteroscopic vision from the posterior wall of the uterus, maintaining a 1 cm margin from any visible intrauterine adhesion. This approach ensured that all samples were collected from bona fide, non-fibrotic endometrium adjacent to the pathological area—tissue most likely to reflect the therapeutic response—while maintaining consistency across timepoints. The posterior wall of the uterine cavity is among the most reproducible and accessible sampling sites, particularly in cases where extensive synechiae may limit access to other regions. Hysteroscopic guidance allowed us to avoid areas of severe fibrosis or necrosis that would preclude meaningful histological evaluation, focusing instead on viable tissue with regenerative potential. Furthermore, the literature acknowledges the existence of different adhesion types (fibrous, muscular, or mixed) that cause variable degrees of damage across the uterine cavity (Foix A et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol, 1966). Our approach accounted for this variability by consistently sampling from the perilesional functional endometrium, which is most relevant for evaluating the impact of cell therapy aimed at tissue regeneration. In summary, while the entire endometrium may be variably affected in IUA, our standardized and targeted biopsy strategy ensured comparability of samples before and after treatment, thereby strengthening the reliability of our histological assessments. The rationale for performing stem cell treatment in mid-secretory phase is because progesterone essentially creates a “fertile ground” for the stem cells to recognize, adhere, engraft, and contribute to regeneration. Progesterone transforms the estrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory, receptive state. This includes decidualization of stromal fibroblasts, increased extracellular matrix deposition, and altered immune tolerance. Also, P4 upregulates angiogenic factors such as VEGF and angiopoietins, which make the microvasculature more permeable to circulating cells. In this primed environment, progesterone also induces expression of key chemotactic and adhesion molecules—including CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins—that are critical for guiding stem cells toward the endometrial tissue. Finally, P induces expression of factors like CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins, which guide stem cells toward the endometrial tissue (1-9). Stem cells administered via intravascular injection in uterine microcirculation can reach the spiral arterioles and venules of the endometrium. They express surface receptors such as CXCR4, which respond to progesterone-induced chemokine gradients, facilitating active homing and targeted migration into the stromal compartment. Progesterone-induced endothelial changes further support stem cell adhesion, rolling, and diapedesis into the tissue. Once engrafted, stem cells secrete growth factors (e.g., HGF, IGF-1, bFGF) that enhance epithelial proliferation, angiogenesis, and stromal repair. In some instances, mesenchymal stem cells may differentiate into endometrial stromal-like cells, replenishing damaged areas. Both progesterone and stem cells both promote a locally anti-inflammatory, pro regenerative environment, reducing fibrosis and allowing structural regeneration (10). Importantly, if stem cells were injected without progesterone priming, the endometrium may remain in a proliferative or atrophic state with lower vascular permeability, less chemokine signaling, and reduced receptivity, impairing stem cell engraftment and therapeutic efficacy. The rationale for evaluation in the mid-secretory phase is because this part of the menstrual cycle represents the most informative time point for clinical evaluation of endometrial receptivity improvements following stem cell therapy. This window allows for the assessment of key surrogate markers, including endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. These parameters provide measurable evidence of structural and functional regeneration. Reviewer #1 (Remarks on code availability): n/a Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author): Thank you for the improvements to the manuscript. The overall organization has clearly progressed, so that analyses for AS patients, organoids, CD133+, CellChat, and differential abundance/expression are now easier to navigate. As a minor addition, a brief, targeted cleanup of the repo could reach a higher level of transparency and reusability that will greatly benefit readers. Here, I would recommend adding a stepwise analysis scheme directly in the README as a small table to anchor timelines and versions for Data collection window, QC/processing window, Figure generation, and Manuscript freeze. This makes it more comprehensible which code/outputs map to the results in the manuscript and helps future users reuse the analyses tied to a specific manuscript freeze (the one from 2023 or the potentially upcoming one). Please cite it prominently in the README and in the relevant scripts, and briefly note what was adopted or extended (e.g., “CellChat settings and epithelial subpopulation markers adapted from …”). This avoids ambiguity and situates your work in the existing literature, even if its your own. Please also check again for hard-coded elements that reduce portability, e.g. replace absolute paths, inline parameters, and environment-specific toggles. with a single config.yml (paths, sample IDs, thresholds). (Example found in https://github.com/FCS-BioIT/asherman-trial-cd133-cell-therapy-public/blob/main/src/R/AS_Patients/maester/analyze_variants/explore_variants_final.r) You could also commit an environment spec (R: renv.lock via renv::snapshot() or a minimal DESCRIPTION; Python: requirements.txt / environment.yml if applicable).
