### Reviewer 1

Review of the article by Santamaria et al “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial’. The authors are reporting a non-randomized prospective open label trial on autologous hematopoetic stem cell therapy for Asherman syndrome cases resistant to existing therapies. The group has been working on the possibility of such therapy for over a decade now, and while this approach is cumbersome, expensive and possibly not available for many, it is an important pathophysiology driven treatment that has a potential. I want to commend on use of lineage tracing experiments showing the engraftment of the CD133+ cells, and on demonstrated changes in the cell populations by single-cell RNA seq studies. Please see comments below. Comments: 1. Line 114, “the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse event…”. What do you mean? You mean this was the most serious adverse event? It was only in 1 patient, and what about chest pain or bleeding? 2. I suggest adding “infection” to the causes of AS. 3. I recommend presenting the data on menstrual pattern and its recovery (before and after the treatment) in the text clearer and in Table 1 (or separately). It is an important clinical information. Provide reference for menstrual pictogram. 4. Make sure it is clear in the Abstract and text that hysteroscopy was only diagnostic, no lysis of adhesions was performed, to be able to truly evaluate the effect of the therapy. This is really not clear. 5. Table 1 and text: you did not present pregnancy rates and miscarriage rates, just live births. How many transfers were performed per patient and in total to get the 6 live births? 6. Lines 164-166: these conclusions should be softer as clinical significance is not clear, if any. What about difference in delta from pre- to post- in these measures? 7. Line 182: what do you mean by uterine curettage was performed by operative hysteroscopy? Do you want to say that retained products of conception were removed hysteroscopically? I do hope that uterine curettage was not performed in this AS patient. 8. Single-cell RNA seq results: why would AS-epithelial cells increase after cell therapy? Aren’t they being replaced more by epithelial cells? 9. Analysis of unique mtDNA: why only 2 patients? Also, in the text you mention only 2 patient samples, but in Figure 4E and figure legend its 3 patients, unless I am getting it wrong. 10. When you get to organoids, the description of results is more chaotic and you are losing the reader. 11. What are the in vivo controls? 12. I am not sure how you showed the improved receptivity, that’s an overstatement. 13. What are the future directions? Are the authors proposing large clinical trial (RCT) or to move this therapy to clinic now, without phase 3? Not clear how this will look like. Should mention the associated health care costs and alternatives, as well as interdisciplinary approach involved in this treatment. 14. Figure 3: why didn’t you present all 19 patients that completed the treatment and post-treatment evaluations? 15. Who was performing the hysteroscopies, before and after the treatment? Were clinicians blinded to the therapy timing such as did they know that they are doing pre- or post-stem cell therapy cavity assessment? How was their bias managed? 16. When was the endometrial thickness measured, in which cycle phase? I understand that these are moderate-severe AS patients, but if you want this study to be taken seriously, you have to be consistent in when the lining thickness is measured. Where in the menstrual cycle were the 2D and 3D evaluations done, hysteroscopy and then the stem cell treatment? If amenorrhea, cycle phase could have been assessed by scanning ovaries and hormonal testing. 17. Table 1: why NA for endometrial volume assessment in 3 patients? 18. Table 2: I suggest using “false passage instead of “false path”. “Bleeding”- what is it, uterine/vaginal or intraabdominal? Vomiting (not vomit. What is Abdominal swelling, is it hives on the skin, or bloating? You should be more specific about skin rash, just localized or generalized? Also, is arm pain same as pain associated with arm hematoma? What is respiratory infection, just URI or something more serious? 19. Was the brachial artery catheterization done under anesthesia or procedural cedation? Minor comments: 1. Some language revision is recommended for sentence flow, and some typos and missing words. 2. Sentence on lines 76-79: please revise, not too clear. 3. In the Results, please be consistent when writing pre-AS, pre-treatment AS or AS-pre- and -post. Both in the text and Figures. 4. Discussion, line 306: are your references 17-23 or 28 as stated? Reference list goes to 23 only.

### Reviewer 2

The authors reported the safety and efficacy of intrauterine intravascular injection of bone marrow-derived CD133+ stem cells in treating 20 cases of refractory Asherman syndrome. Single-cell sequencing of endometrial tissues from a subset of cases before and after treatment was performed to investigate the stem cell homing and differentiation，and transcriptional profile changes of the administered cells in vivo, as well as organoid formation capacity and associated expression alterations. While the study is interesting and holds significant clinical relevance, several critical aspects require further elucidation to strengthen its translational impact. 1. In the research proposal, this research was described as a prospective, multicenter, and self-controlled study. However, the current report appears to be based on work conducted at a single center. Could you please provide the reasons? 2.Result 1 On line 94, the author states that “Following diagnostic hysteroscopy, hematopoietic stem cells were mobilized, harvested through leukapheresis, and selected for CD133+ and intra-endometrial spiral arterioles instillation (Fig. 1A).” Was surgical separation of intrauterine adhesions required before injection? In which phase of the menstrual cycle should the injection be administered? 3.How was the cell therapy dosage determined? Was it simply based on the amount of cells that could be isolated and obtained? 4.In secondary endpoint, I noticed that the specific location of the endometrial biopsy for comparing histological changes and immunohistochemical staining before and after treatment seems to be missing in the methodology section. Could you please provide more details on this aspect? 5.In the legend of Fig. 2, the sample sizes indicated for the box plots of endometrial volume (n=16) and endometrial thickness (n=19) appear to be inconsistent with the figure itself. It is possible that there might be a typographical error by the author. Why are the sample sizes for the analysis of endometrial thickness and endometrial volume different—one being 16 cases and the other 19 cases—when the total sample size should be 20 cases? 6.Regarding the efficacy, the key efficacy endpoint is the live birth rate. From Table 1, it appears that successful pregnancy mainly depends on the severity of the disease. Could the author address this point in the manuscript? 7.On line 256, the author states that “RNA-based UMAP clustering post-treatment demonstrated the presence of CD133+ mtDNA clones within diverse endometrial cell populations (Figure 4E), confirming the grafting and multilineage differentiation capacity of CD133+ BMDSC post-cell therapy.” However, it may be necessary to have experimental evidence to confirm the differentiation capacity of CD133+ BMDSC, rather than relying solely on the findings from single-cell sequencing. The viability of the cells used for treatment was >50%. Could it be that dead cells entered the body, their mitochondrial DNA was engulfed or phagocytosed by other cells, rather than differentiating into other cell types? 8.The author selected endometrial samples from nine patients before and after treatment for subsequent single-cell sequencing analysis. However, the author did not explain the criteria for selecting these nine cases. The relevant clinical information for these nine patients should be provided. Additionally, the results of the single-cell sequencing need to be validated experimentally. 9.In Single-cell RNA sequencing of endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs) derived from endometrial biopsies pre- and post-treatment，the clinical information of the patients from whom the organoids were derived should be provided. 10.In discussion part, to facilitate readers' understanding of the progress in stem cell therapy for Asherman's syndrome, the author would provide a brief and objective overview of the published studies. When emphasizing the strengths of this research, the author mentions the use of "a specific, well-characterized cell" for treatment. However, based on the "methods" section, the purity of the cells used is about 70%. What about the remaining 30%? What types of cells do they consist of, and what is their impact on endometrial regeneration? It would be best if the author could clarify this.

### Reviewer 3

This study titled ‘Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase1/2 trial’ by Xavier Santamaria et al., present promising results on the use of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells (BMDSCs) for treating Asherman Syndrome (AS), a condition with limited treatment options. I have several questions and comments listed below that need to be answered by the authors. My major points are these and further details follows below: Major points: Without a control group/placebo, interpreting the real effectiveness of the intervention is very difficult because you lack a baseline for comparison in stage 2. The main limitation of this study is that the data are limited to only one-month post-transplantation, which is not sufficient to assess the long-term safety and efficacy of the treatment. Extended follow-up, ideally up to the trial’s defined 15-month endpoint is necessary to support the conclusions. Additionally, the absence of a control group makes it difficult to confidently attribute observed effects to the treatment. While the hysteroscopic images provide some information, their value is limited due to variation in sampling location, unknown menstrual cycle phase and inconsistent hormone levels during the first month. These factors introduce variability and make it hard to draw firm conclusions from the histological data. 1. For the 20 patients recruited to the study, they all underwent reparative operative hysteroscopies (range 1 to 11). During how long time was treatment attempted? 2. Authors mentioned that despite the previous surgical treatments, no patients reported improvement of endometrial thickness. Did they not receive conventional hormonal therapy after the previous operation? 3. After the cell transplantation, have you considered administered estrogen supplement? 4. For the secondary endpoints, authors stated that ‘pretreatment patient menstrual blood loss was around 29.6ml increasing to 55.2ml in the first month post-treatment, however, decreased to 31.1ml and 29.9ml in third and fifth month post-treatment. What could be the reason for this? In addition, you recruited moderate to severe AS patients, these patients are most likely amenorrheic or spotting. What is the menstrual conditions pre-treatment for these patients? There is no information in Table 1. 5. Regarding the dose range (37–166.1 × 10⁶ cells): Was this range selected based on prior studies, or was it a dose-escalation design? The rationale for the wide range should be clarified. 6.Reversible Limb Paresthesia: This is an interesting and somewhat unexpected adverse event. Further discussion on the mechanism would be valuable. 7. No haemopoietic malignancies were reported. For how long will the patients be followed and what is known regarding this risk? 8.Endometrial Improvements: authors reported increases in thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores are encouraging. Was there a correlation between cell dose and response/duration of effect? 9. The authors mentioned a key outcome about reproductive endometrial function recovery. It includes 6 Live Births and 6 miscarriages. Before the cell transplantation treatment did these patients also receive embryo transfer? 10. How many Et attempts per patient? More than one? 11. The authors added mechanistic Insights by applying Single-cell RNA Sequencing before and after treatment. In the previous paper (Santamaria X, et al. 2023), authors identified two unique cell types only present in AS (AS epithelium and smooth muscle cells). The cells isolated for scRNA-seq most likely came from superficial layer of the endometrium. Do authors think that severe AS are more related to damaged basalis layer? In that case the mechanistic study would need to include basalis tissue to truly reveal the efficacy and underlying mechanism. 12.The finding of "partial reversion of AS-related changes" is intriguing but vague. Were there specific gene pathways or cell populations most affected except for the increase of several cell types? What about the post-treatment changes of the two AS unique cell types? 13. For the organoid part, the organoids were hormone-treated in vitro. The three controls—were they age-/fertility-matched to AS patients? If not, differences could reflect baseline variability rather than treatment effects. 14. Regarding the organoid sequencing results, the increase in proliferative EMT cells post-treatment is intriguing but raises questions: Is this proliferative shift a direct effect of CD133+ BMDSCs (e.g., via paracrine signaling) or an indirect consequence of endometrial repair? Could excessive EMT proliferation risk fibrosis or aberrant regeneration? The authors should discuss whether this profile aligns with healthy endometrial repair. 15: Figure 3 presents hysteroscopic images before and after treatment for all participants, which is well appreciated. However, it is not specified on which day of the menstrual cycle these images were taken, nor how many days post-treatment they were obtained. From Table 1, it appears but not clear that participants were not amenorrheic. Could the authors clarify the timing of image acquisition in relation to the menstrual cycle and the treatment timeline? This information is particularly important considering the statement in lines 148–150, which notes an increase in menstrual blood flow during the first month after treatment, returning to pre-treatment levels after three months. Was this temporal pattern in blood flow reflected in the hysteroscopic findings? 16. Considering the transient increase in menstrual blood flow during the first month post-treatment, it would be informative to include hysteroscopic images from three months after treatment in non-pregnant women to assess long-term endometrial changes. 17. In reference to lines 143–150, the authors state that menstrual blood loss increased during the first month post-treatment but returned to pre-treatment levels after three months. Does this suggest that the underlying condition was not fully resolved, given that the menstrual pattern ultimately reverted to its baseline state? If normal menstrual cycling resumed or improved, one might expect a sustained change in menstrual pattern or blood flow, especially considering the reported increase in endometrial thickness after treatment (lines 127–133, Figure 2B, and Table 1). Could the authors clarify how this temporal pattern in menstrual blood loss corresponds to treatment efficacy and the overall resolution of the syndrome? 18: The scale bar in Supplementary Figure 3 for the gene expression data needs to be corrected for accurate interpretation. 19: Tissue samples were collected pre- and post-treatment from nine participants, and the data in Figure 5A suggest that at least three samples were used to generate 3D organoids. For clarity and completeness, it would be helpful to include representative 3D organoid data from all nine participants if performed, or at minimum the three samples that were analyzed and presented in figure 5 A, like the presentation style in Figure 2, to allow assessment of inter-patient variability and enhance data transparency. 20. For the organoid part, the organoids were hormone-treated in vitro. The three controls—were they age-/fertility-matched to AS patients? If not, differences could reflect baseline variability rather than treatment effects. 21. Regarding the organoid sequencing results, the increase in proliferative EMT cells post-treatment is intriguing but raises questions: Is this proliferative shift a direct effect of CD133+ BMDSCs (e.g., via paracrine signaling) or an indirect consequence of endometrial repair? Could excessive EMT proliferation risk fibrosis or aberrant regeneration? The authors should discuss whether this profile aligns with healthy endometrial repair. 22. It is not indicated when the sample were obtained after the treatment for scRNA and 3D organoids culture. 23: The scRNA-seq data in Supplementary Figure 4E indicate upregulation of angiogenic pathways ANGPTL; to strengthen these findings, it would be valuable to include supporting protein-level validation of key pathway components, such as through immunostaining or western blotting. 24: Mitochondrial Variant Tracking: This is a clever approach to assess engraftment. What percentage of endometrial cells post-treatment showed donor mitochondrial DNA? What is the most abundant cell type that bone marrow stem cells may differentiate into? Did engraftment correlate with clinical outcomes? The use of mtDNA for lineage tracing is powerful but not sure how mitochondrial transfer between cells via mechanisms such as tunneling nanotubes, cell fusion, or exosome-mediated exchange affects the clonality. These events can introduce exogenous mtDNA, potentially leading to misinterpretation of clonal relationships. 25. line 196-199 concludes that perivascular cells increase after the treatment and Macrophage decreases, need some comments in discussion about this. It's not clear how pericytes are involved in endometrium but in CNS it's very well accepted that pericytes forms the scar tissue after injury and inhibits regeneration. 26: Protein validation for the genes has not been presented, only RNA data was shown. It would be valuable to present how the AS epithelial cells change after treatment and how the scar/perivascular cells are affected.

### Reviewer 4

Comments on “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial” As requested by the Editor, our review will be limited to those aspects that relate to the trial design and statistics of this manuscript. We do not have sufficient experience and knowledge for evaluation of aspects that are more specific to cells and laboratory work. Considering that Asherman Syndrome has a significant impact on the quality of life of many people, and that currently the only possible intervention - which is often not definitive - is operative hysteroscopy, the identification of different approaches could be of great value. This is especially true if these possible new interventions are able to overcome infertility. Therefore, we commend the authors for their commitment to the search for new treatment options. We thus appreciated the authors’ effort in conducting this clinical trial aimed at evaluating the tolerability, safety, and efficacy of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy in patients with Asherman Syndrome (AS) refractory to surgical interventions. Overall, the methodological components of the study are appropriate for a non-randomised, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. We are of the opinion that the study design is well-structured, and we do not have any major comments on this aspect. However, considering that the study represents a complex methodological project integrating clinical and molecular approaches, we believe that some clarifications and further details may be useful, both regarding the objectives of the study and the use of statistics. This is all the more important given that the sample consisted of 20 women (one of whom did not complete the study), which is relatively large considering the prevalence of the disease, but relatively small considering the numerous endpoints set by the authors. We reiterate the importance of this study and offer some comments and suggestions to further improve the clarity, transparency and robustness of the analyses. Major comments 1. Partially addressed primary endpoints According to the trial registration on the European Union Clinical Trial Register (EudraCT: 2016-003975-23), three primary endpoints were declared: “1. Identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur in the patient throughout the study up until Month 15 post-treatment. 2. In the event of a term pregnancy, identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur during the pregnancy, birth and puerperal period. 3. In case of a Live Birth (LB), identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events that may be associated with the investigational medicinal product (IMP) until the first month of age.” However, in the present study, only the first primary endpoint appears to have been thoroughly developed, and its results reported. The results of the primary endpoints are reported in the manuscript on lines 109-116 and in Table 2. There is no mention of primary endpoints 2 and 3, i.e. pregnancies and births. Some information on these is provided in secondary endpoints section and in the supplementary material, but as these are primary endpoints - and therefore theoretically the most important ones - they should be clearly presented in the section of the results dealing with the primary endpoints. It would be appropriate for the authors to complete the analysis by including the remaining two primary endpoints as outlined in the registered protocol. Alternatively, the authors should state why the results of the other two primary endpoints were not reported in the primary endpoint results section and were not discussed. For example, the most outstanding result of this study is mentioned by the authors in the abstract: "...reproductive function was restored, culminating in six live births after embryo transfer". It is not clear why this striking observation is barely mentioned in the manuscript, neither in the results nor in the discussion, even if one of the primary endpoints was the “identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events” in case of a life birth. It is clear that the set of secondary and explanatory outcomes is intended to try to understand the biological and molecular reasons behind the regained fertility of some women. Nevertheless, the primary endpoint is in danger of being obscured by all the other analyses. 2. Excessive detailing of secondary and exploratory endpoints Although the presentation of the results and discussion of the secondary and exploratory endpoints is comprehensive and thorough, the length and level of detail may be reconsidered as it seems disproportionate to the primary objectives of the study. A more concise approach could benefit the overall focus and readability of the manuscript. Alternatively, the endpoints of the study could be refocused. 3. Predictive model based on Support Vector Machine (SVM) In the section concerning endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs), the authors add the use of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) with a kernel radial basis functon(RBF), implemented via the scPred package, to perform transcriptomic comparison with in vivo data. However, although a brief description of the process is provided (10-fold cross-validation and C parameter optimization), several key methodological elements are missing, e.g. the type of learning adopted, the target classes used for model training, the feature selection procedure, the model performance metrics, and the rationale for choosing the RBF kernel, among others. Given the complexity and methodological significance of a machine learning-based analysis, we recommend that a dedicated and detailed methods section be added. Alternatively, since this does not represent one of the study’s primary endpoints, the analysis could be considered for omission. Minor comments 1. Statistical methodology presentation Although the statistical methodology covers a broad range of analyses, it is overall unclear, dispersed, and difficult to follow. The statistical tests used are reported in different sections of the methodology and not always in a systematic manner, making it challenging to obtain a comprehensive view of the analyses performed. We therefore recommend including a more structured and concise section that clearly summarizes all the applied tests, the type of data analysed, and the rationale behind the choice of each statistical test. Alternatively, we suggest including a subsection on the statistics and software used within each section of the methodology. This will allow the reader to better understand the different statistical approaches used. 2. Assumptions behind the use of parametric tests When parametric tests were used instead of non-parametric ones, it is not specified whether the assumption of normality of the data distribution was verified. An example of this is the use of the paired t-test to evaluate the IUA score. Since this is a score, it is likely that nonparametric tests would be more appropriate. Or, if a parametric test is needed, it would be appropriate to state the rationale for such a choice. 3. Choice of statistical test for organoid quantification A two-way ANOVA test was used in the organoid quantification section. It would be useful for the authors to clarify the rationale for using a two-way analysis. A two-way ANOVA analyses the effect of two different categorical independent variables on a continuous dependent variable. It is not clear what the two independent variables are in this case. In addition, it is important to specify whether there were two independent interacting factors. Could it be that a one-way ANOVA would have been more appropriate? 4. Statistical power and sample size calculation The authors calculated the sample size based on a hypothetical increase in live births from 0% to 28%. The hypothesis is probably correct. However, this sample size calculation assumes that the primary objective of the trial is to examine the percentage of women who have a pregnancy that ends in a live birth. For all the other analyses that have been performed, namely those related to secondary and exploratory endpoints, this sample calculation is not as crucial. To give just one example, when it comes to endometrial volume or thickness a sample calculation based on the proportion of life births has no reason to be (even if it is still a paired cohort study). It is sufficient to say that a convenience sample was studied, or the sample size should be computed on a hypothetical difference on volumes or thickness. In any case, in the description of the sample size calculation, the authors do not report the statistical power value used for the estimate. It is recommended that the power and alpha values assumed in the calculation are explicitly reported. 5. Typographical errors. Finally, we suggest a review of, e.g. in the methods section: “Patients were managed as described previously described…”

### Reviewer 5

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 6

General This phase 1/2 trial assessed the safety, efficacy, and biological plausibility of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy for treating moderate to severe Asherman Syndrome (AS) in 20 infertile women unresponsive to prior treatments. The therapy was well-tolerated, with reversible limb paresthesia as the most common side effect. Significant improvements were observed in endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. Clinically, menstruation and reproductive function were restored, leading to six live births following embryo transfer. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed partial reversion of AS-related changes, and mitochondrial variant tracking showed insights into stem cell engraftment. The results suggest this therapy is safe and effective, warranting further investigation in larger trials. The manuscript is well-written, grammatically sound, and addresses a highly interesting topic, combining stem cell applications as orphan drugs with single-cell technologies. However, some technical aspects related to the bioinformatics analyses, such as the use of older packages (CellRanger, Seurat), as well as the provision of analysis scripts, could benefit from refinement. Major 1. How was the concentration of mobilized cells (at least 30 million cells with >70% purity and >50% viability) determined for this study? Is this concentration commonly used for CD133+ BMDSCs in this application? In cardiac regeneration studies, similar cell collections often use lower concentrations, how does this compare to your approach? 2. Could you explain the rationale behind using CellRanger Software version 3.1.0 (from July 2019) for this analysis, given that the current version is 9.0.1? Additionally, I noticed that Seurat version 4 was used, whereas version 5 is available for quite some time. The use of these older versions, both for CellRanger and Seurat, can potentially result in different analysis outcomes due to improvements or changes in data processing and downstream analysis methods introduced in newer versions. 3. Did the authors also perform quality assessments using tools like MultiQC to aggregate the overall quality of the samples? It might be beneficial to provide these quality reports as supplemental material to account for the sequencing quality. 4. Did the authors also perform dataset integration using Harmony (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0619-0) in addition to the SCT transformation, which is commonly considered a standard approach for handling batch effects, particularly when samples have been processed in different batches? While Harmony is mentioned in the methods section, it appears to be described within the machine learning part, rather than in the single-cell processing section. Could you clarify when Harmony was applied in the analysis and why it was not used in all experiments? 5. Could you please include the cell-to-cell communication analyses in the methods section? 6. Providing the relevant scripts in a public repository would greatly enhance the overall reproducibility and depths of the data analysis. Minor 1. The required number of patients is inconsistent between the methods section and the study protocol, 20 versus 22. It may be helpful for the authors and readers to standardize and use a single number throughout the entire work. 2. The authors also may provide the exact version of the genome build used GRCh38-3.0.0. 3. Did the authors used specific databases, tools or scientific literature to annotate the single cell clusters - Reference 3 in the main manuscript (results) might be added also in the methods section in more detail, if the annotation is mainly based on previous works of the authors, including the species under investigation (e.g., murine, cell-based, …). 4. How was the selection of the 9 out of 20 patients was conducted for the single-cell analysis? 5. Please remove the “.” In the middle of the sentence in line 327.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy has been designated as an Orphan Drug by the EMA and FDA for the treatment of Asherman Syndrome (AS). This phase 1/2, non-randomized, open-label, single-arm trial assessed the safety and efficacy of this novel therapy in 20 infertile women with moderate to severe AS, unresponsive to prior hysteroscopic treatments. Primary endpoints were safety and tolerability over 15 months follow-up, including during pregnancy and after live birth. The therapy was well tolerated with a mean dosage of 125.41×10^6 cells, with no treatment-related serious adverse events and only reversible events such as arm pain, headache, and nausea. In pregnant patients, minor obstetric complications were reflux-related cough (n=1), gestational diabetes (n=2), cervical shortening requiring pessary placement (n=2), and postpartum placenta accreta (n=1). No preterm labor occurred, and all six newborns remained free of significant adverse events. Our findings suggest that autologous CD133+ BMDSC therapy is a safe and effective treatment for AS. Clinical trial registration (EudraCT): 2016-003975-23

---

## Introduction

Asherman Syndrome (AS) is an acquired pathological condition affecting women’s reproductive health, triggered by the substitution of a bona fide endometrium with intrauterine adhesions (IUAs) that cause the uterine walls to adhere to each other. Clinically, AS results in menstrual abnormalities (amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea), pelvic pain, infertility, recurrent miscarriage and abnormal placentation1. The onset of AS is mainly caused by procedures such as postpartum curettage of the uterine cavity, after miscarriage and/or infection. These events can disrupt the endometrial niche where progenitor/stem cells may reside2 causing a significant reduction in endometrial epithelial compartment and a dysfunctional pro-fibrotic, pro-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic environment3.

Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the current standard treatment with limited clinical results, especially in the moderate and severe stages4–6. Advanced cell therapies have emerged as a potential therapy for AS aiming to treat with cells what cannot be treated by drugs7. Specifically, autologous CD133+ bone marrow derived stem cells (BMDSCs) were initially used to treat AS in a murine model of AS8,9. Then, a proof-of-concept trial provided preliminary evidence of the safety and therapeutic benefit of this investigational product in patients with moderate/severe AS refractory to operative hysteroscopy treatments10. As a result, autologous CD133+ BMDSCs were granted Orphan Drug designation for the treatment of AS by both the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)11.

We present a 15-month follow-up study from a non-randomized, open-label, phase 1/2 trial for 20 patients experiencing clinical symptoms including infertility, due to moderate or severe AS according to the IUAs ASRM classification12, those who are refractory to operative hysteroscopy treatments. Here, we describe the safety, effectiveness in terms of therapeutic outcomes, and biological plausibility at single cell level of autologous CD133+ BMDSC treatment.

---

## Results

Participant identification and baseline characteristics
This is a prospective, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized, phase 1/2 trial, in which we enrolled infertile patients with a hysteroscopic diagnosis of moderate or severe AS according to the IUAs ASRM classification12. This clinical trial involved administration of an advanced therapy medicinal product (ATMP) during the simulated secretory phase (5 days after progesterone administration), where the use of autologous CD133+ BMDSCs was approved by the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS, April 20th, 2020) and the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at the Hospital Universitari Vall D’Hebron Barcelona, Spain (April 17th, 2020, IGX1-ENT-XS-16-01).

Following diagnostic hysteroscopy, hematopoietic stem cells were mobilized, harvested through leukapheresis, and selected for CD133+ before intra-endometrial spiral arterioles instillation. Although the minimum accepted range of mobilized cells was at least 30 million cells with a >70% purity and >50% viability, the average of CD133+ instilled cells was 125.41×10^6 cells with a purity of 89.54±8.29%, and a viability of 99.7±0.27%, exceeding minimum thresholds. An overview of the study design is described in Fig. 1A.

Between September 7th, 2020 and September 19th, 2022, 24 patients were screened for eligibility, 20 were enrolled and received autologous CD133+ BMDSC therapy (Fig. 1B). A detailed summary of clinical characteristics of participants pre- and post-AS therapy is presented in Table 1.

The mean age of patients was 38.3 years (IQR 37.5–40). The average number of previously attempted reparative operative hysteroscopies was 3.2 (range 1 to 11). Despite previous surgical treatments, no patient reported significant improvement of their endometrial thickness, volume, hysteroscopic scores, and none had achieved pregnancy after AS was diagnosed (Table 1).

Primary endpoints
The primary endpoints of this study were to evaluate safety and tolerability of this autologous cell therapy with up to 15 months follow-up, during pregnancy and in cases of live birth. The therapy was well tolerated at doses ranging from 37 to 166.1×10^6 cells (mean dosage 125.41×10^6 cells). No serious adverse events related to the medicinal product were observed and no haemopoietic malignancies were reported. The most common adverse events after stem cell administration included arm pain, headache and nausea, which in all cases were mild and reversible. Arm pain was mostly related to catheterization and was solved with local ice administration. A detailed list of adverse events is presented in Table 2.

Among the pregnant patients, no serious adverse events were observed beyond common obstetric complications. One patient experienced a persistent cough attributed to gastroesophageal reflux. Two patients developed gestational diabetes, which was successfully managed through dietary interventions. Cervical shortening requiring pessary placement occurred in two cases. Additionally, one patient presented placenta accreta after delivery, requiring manual placental extraction and blood transfusion. Notably, there were no cases of preterm labor and no significant adverse events were reported in the six newborns during the first month of life.

Secondary endpoints
The secondary endpoints included endometrial morphometry, thickness, volume, uterine hysteroscopic scores, and endometrial function evaluated by menstruation recovery and pregnancy outcomes. Endometrial morphometry was obtained from the biopsies extracted analyzed by digital analysis of H&E-stained endometrial biopsy sections before and one month after therapy (Supplementary Fig. 1A). After cell therapy, we observed a 62% increase in gland percentage, a 64% reduction in fiber-rich stroma, and a 73% increase in vessel percentage within the stroma. Additionally, a statistically significant decrease in gland area and gland lumen was noted (Supplementary Fig. 1A).

Analysis on endometrial thickness showed an improvement in all patients analyzed (Fig. 2A) from the maximal value of 4.90 mm (range 3–4.9 mm) with a mean of 3.80±0.95 mm pre-AS therapy to a maximal thickness post-AS therapy of 6.50 mm (range 4-6.5 mm) with a mean value of 5.29±0.77 mm (p<0.05) (Fig. 2B, Table 1). Endometrial volume as assessed by 3D ultrasound also increased in all patients (Fig. 2A) with a mean of 1.26 cm³ (range 0.27-3.5 cm³) before, versus 2.78 cm³ (range 0.48–4.9 cm³) after cell therapy (p<0.05) (Fig. 2C, Table 1).

Hysteroscopic scores according to the IUAs ASRM classification12 performed before (pre-AS therapy) and approximately one month after cell therapy (post-AS therapy), revealed improvements in the endometrium and the uterine cavity for the patients (Fig. 3A). IUAs score pre-AS therapy was 8.0±3.17, whereas post-AS therapy was reduced to 4.42±2.09 (p<0.0001, Fig. 3B). More specifically, 6 out of 8 severe AS cases improved to moderate stage, 1 improved to mild stage and 1 remained as severe but with a better score. From the rest of the 12 moderate AS patients, 8 improved to a mild stage and 4 improved their IUA to a moderate score.

Endometrial function post-AS therapy was assessed clinically by the recovery of menstrual function in terms of pictorial blood loss assessment, as previously reported13. We used a validated menstrual pictogram to measure total menstrual blood loss as described in methods based on the number and staining of tampons and/or menstrual pads used per menstrual period. Each score is comparable to a milliliter of blood loss. Most patients did not have their period prior to the treatment and so menstrual blood records were prospectively assessed after therapy (1–6 months), as stated per protocol. Menstrual blood loss records showed an increase from 29.60±45.40 mL in the first month post-therapy to 56.66±107.41 mL after 2 months post-therapy. Data showed then a decrease in the records, with 27.66±19.79 mL in the last month after treatment (M6) (Table 3).

As per the reproductive outcomes among the 20 treated patients, one live birth resulted from a spontaneous pregnancy post-therapy and 5 live births resulted after ARTs. In total, we performed a total of 41 single embryo transfers in 19 patients yielding an implantation rate of 31.7% per embryo transferred (13/41). Out of these transfers, as stated above, we obtained 5 live births corresponding to a 12.19% of life birth rate per transfer attempt. When analyzed per patient, the cumulative pregnancy rate was 55% (11/20), and the cumulative live birth rate was 30% (6/20) (Table 1). Interestingly, the patients who achieved a live birth had been diagnosed with moderate stage AS, suggesting that treatment efficacy may be influenced by disease severity. However, given the small sample size and data heterogeneity—the unequal distribution of moderate and severe cases—this observation should be considered preliminary.

The analysis of associations between pre- and post-AS therapy changes in endometrial volume, thickness, IUA scores, and morphometry revealed statistically significant differences between patients who achieved live birth (LB) and those who experienced miscarriage. Specifically, LB was significantly associated with post-AS therapy increases in endometrial volume and thickness (Supplementary Fig. 1B). In contrast, the miscarriage group exhibited significant changes in endometrial thickness and IUA scores (Supplementary Fig. 1C). These findings suggest that achieving an endometrial thickness of approximately 5.46±0.89 mm and an endometrial volume of around 3.62±0.85 cm³ may be associated with improved live birth outcomes in this study. Although we showed a potential association between enhanced endometrial characteristics and improved reproductive outcomes, it is important to note that live birth outcomes are also influenced by embryo transfer–related factors, such as embryo quality, number of transfers, timing, etc. These elements likely interact to determine overall success and need to be taken into consideration.

Associations between obstetrical outcomes revealed that the time range to achieve a successful pregnancy was 77 to 313.7 days (75% CI) (Supplementary Fig. 1D). Regarding dosage, no statistically significant differences were observed between pregnant and non-pregnant patients in terms of the number of CD133+ BMDSC cells administered, which ranged from 37 to 166.1×10^6 cells (75% CI) (Supplementary Fig. 1E).

As per endometrial functionality obtained (obstetrical outcomes), three out of six deliveries were performed by cesarean section and there were 3 vaginal deliveries. All deliveries were at term (range 37–38.6 W). All the newborns had normal weights (mean 3399 gr; range 3040–3970 gr) and normal development at one month. None displayed any signs of infection and there were no recorded congenital abnormalities. One of the participants experienced a first-trimester miscarriage that required hysteroscopic removal of the retained products of conception.

Exploratory endpoints
Single-cell RNA sequencing of the AS endometrium pre- and post-AS therapy. Previously, we published the AS endometrial cell atlas at single-cell resolution describing syndrome-associated alterations in cell types, cell-to-cell communication and gene expression profiles that supported a dysfunctional pro-fibrotic, pro-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic environment3. We had previously characterized the transcriptomic profile of AS (pre-AS therapy) and identified up to 18 cell types, including two unique cell types only present in AS (AS epithelium-SLPI+ and a population of smooth muscle cells). These same patients, who received CD133+ stem cell treatment during the simulated secretory phase, are now presented in the current study with both pre- and post-AS therapy endometrial biopsies (nine out of the 20 enrolled patients, Supplementary Fig. 2A). In parallel, we also performed single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) profiling of the CD133+ product, which revealed a heterogeneous composition consistent with mobilized progenitor cell populations (Supplementary Fig. 2B).

For the endometrial biopsies, scRNA-seq yielded 123,250 cells (40,336 pre-AS therapy vs. 82,914 post-AS therapy, Fig. 4A, Supplementary Fig. 2C). We integrated matched pre-treatment (pre-AS therapy) and post-treatment (post-AS therapy) samples into the same dimensional reduction depiction. Overall, we observed a tendency towards an increase on the epithelial, stromal, endothelial and perivascular compartments (Fig. 4A, Supplementary Fig. 2D, E), a significantly reduced AS-characteristic epithelium (0.22% vs. 0.017%), and decreased macrophage populations (0.61% vs. 0.21%) (Fig. 4A, C). Notably, we previously showed that AS-epithelial population expresses high levels of SLPI3. When comparing the SLPI signal in pre and post-AS therapy samples, we observed that fluorescence was markedly reduced in post-AS therapy samples, which may account for the decrease in this cell population following CD133+ BMDSC treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2F).

We also determined the differential gene expression between pre- and post-AS therapy in different cell types related to a gene set associated to endometrial function (see Methods). The results revealed that epithelial, AS-epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and PV cells presented a higher expression of the gene set after CD133+ BMDSCs treatment, suggesting that cell treatment reactivates endometrial functionality (Fig. 4B). Further differential gene expression evaluation between pre- and post-AS therapy in epithelial cells revealed an increase in post-AS therapy samples of SCGB1D2 (related to functional secretory activity), PDGFRA and IGF1, associated with extracellular matrix remodeling and regeneration. We also observed the reduced expression of S100A10 and genes related to inflammation and immune response in post-treatment epithelial cells. These gene expression differences suggest that autologous cell therapy in the AS endometrium induces the appearance of an epithelium with reduced immune activity and inflammation and restores secretory and regenerative functions. The stromal cell cluster in the AS endometrium after autologous cell therapy exhibited the upregulated expression of genes related to angiogenesis and vascular development such as IGFBP2 and PTN (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Analysis of the endothelial compartment indicated a transcriptomic shift from a pro-inflammatory profile characterized by cell stress to a more homeostatic state (Supplementary Fig. 3). We observed the downregulation of genes involved in leukocyte/myeloid trans-endothelial migration (ICAM), antigen presentation (HLA-DRA and HLA-DRB5), cell proliferation (FOS and JUNB) or heat shock proteins (HSPH1 and HSPA1B). Furthermore, IGFBP2 overexpression suggested the enhanced formation of new blood vessels, and the expression of different collagen genes (e.g., COL1A1, COL3A1) indicated ECM cell adhesion and the development of capillaries from vessels surroundings.

Cell-to-cell communication (CCC) analysis related to immune response and pro-inflammatory pathways revealed a post-AS therapy enrichment in TWEAK, CX3C, IGF and GDF (Fig. 4D) and a reduced in strength after CD133+ BMDSC administration in RESISTIN, IL4, ICAM and LIGHT (Fig. 4D). Within the LIGHT pathway, we observed a disruption in established CCC between CD8+ T cells and various cell types (including stroma, epithelium, endothelium, PV, and immune cells), which was accompanied by a decline in LIGHT signaling between MAIT and stromal cells (Supplementary Fig. 4A). Pre-AS therapy samples also displayed IL4 and RESISTIN signaling pathway activation, which suggested a strong immune activity AS endometrium. Importantly, CD133+ BMDSC administration prompted the loss of these signaling pathways, contributing to the restoration of a homeostatic environment in the endometrium (Supplementary Fig. 4B, C).

Endometrial regeneration after damage has been linked to the activity of the canonical and non-canonical WNT pathways. In this case, CD133+ BMDSC administration prompted the recovery of CCC between the stroma, epithelium, and contractile cells in the WNT signaling pathway (Supplementary Fig. 4D).

Angiogenic pathways involving ANGPTL showed notable changes in CCC interactions following CD133+ BMDSC therapy (Supplementary Fig. 4E). Specifically, we observed a shift toward increased ANGPTL2-mediated interactions in the post-AS therapy group which was validated by immunofluorescence (Supplementary Fig. 4E, F). Given that a balance between ANGPTL1 and ANGPTL2 is critical for angiogenesis and vascular regeneration regulation, the increased ANGPTL2 signaling may reflect a regenerative response induced by the therapy.

Overall, CCC data suggested that CD133+ BMDSC therapy partially restores epithelial populations to a healthier state, enhances cell functionality by reducing oxidative stress and inflammation and promotes angiogenesis.

Lineage tracing differentiation of engrafted CD133+ cells. To track grafting and differentiation of infused CD133+ BMDSCs after cell therapy, we identified unique mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants present in CD133+ BMDSCs before therapy, which were subsequently detected in various differentiated endometrial cell lineages post-therapy. Mitochondrial alteration enrichment from single-cell transcriptomes (MAESTER) was utilized for this analysis to establish relatedness14. Since the MAESTER technique requires reamplification of residual cDNA from single-cell RNA sequencing libraries, we had sufficient high-quality cDNA to perform the analysis in only three patients (N7, N9, and N15). Comprehensive profiling in these three patients revealed 32, 9 and 2 shared mtDNA variants in the endometrium post-treatment, respectively, all of which were absent before the stem cell therapy. RNA-based UMAP clustering post-treatment demonstrated the presence of CD133+ mtDNA clones within diverse endometrial cell populations (Fig. 4E), confirming the grafting and multilineage differentiation capacity of CD133+ BMDSC post-cell therapy.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs) derived from endometrial biopsies pre- and post-AS therapy. We also profiled endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs) from pre- and post-AS therapy and controls at the single-cell level to compare this model with our in vivo data. We collected pre- and post-therapy endometrial samples from three AS patients and three controls (see supplementary data 1), generated EEOs and passaged them twice to remove stromal cell contamination (Fig. 5A). Data showed a significant enhancement in organoid-forming capacity (measured as the number of EEOs generated from the same number of cells) in control and post-AS therapy EEOs compared to pre-AS therapy EEOs (p<0.05). After passage 2, the organoid-forming capacity of cells from the three conditions displayed no significant differences, suggesting the positive selection of organoid-forming cells after 2 passages (Fig. 5A).

scRNA-seq of progesterone-treated EEOs yielded transcriptomic profiles from 49,609 cells in total: 14,459, pre-AS therapy, 19,556, post-AS therapy and 15,594 for controls. Seven populations were identified, consistent with previously characterized AS-derived epithelial organoids3, including glandular, glandular secretory, ciliated, cycling cells (cycling org), proliferative KRT19+, proliferative EMT and KRT17+ cells (Fig. 5B).

In terms of cell percentage, post-AS therapy EEOs showed a higher proportion of proliferative EMT and KRT9 cells than control EEOs and pre-AS therapy EEOs, which could suggest an enhanced proliferative capacity after therapy, although the trend was non-significant. Notably, the ratio glandular secretory/glandular was similar for post-AS therapy EEOs and control EEO (ratio 3.22 and 3.69, respectively), whereas the ratio remained lower for pre-AS therapy (ratio 1.03). Although the proportions of post-AS therapy do not fully mirror those of healthy controls, the shift in epithelial glandular composition after treatment may indicate a trend toward functional remodeling, including an enrichment of cells with a potentially more receptive-like profile (Fig. 5C). These results suggest that EEOs represent a useful in vitro model for studying AS, demonstrating partial recovery of AS EEOs after CD133+ BMDSC therapy to a state resembling control EEOs.
