## Methods

Study design and patients
This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. The trial was registered at the European Union Clinical Trials Register (EU-CTR, EudraCT: 2016-003975-23; Registration date: April 1stst, 2020; https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2016-003975-23/ES), and the Spanish Clinical Studies Registry (REec, https://reec.aemps.es/reec/estudio/2016-003975-23). The investigational medical product (IMP) autologous CD133+ Bone Marrow Derived Stem Cells (BMDSC) was designated as an Orphan Drug (OD) by the EMA on April 20th, 2017 (EMA/OD/313/16)11 and by the FDA on February 1st, 2019 (#DRU-2017-6131). For the design of this clinical trial, scientific advice and protocol assistance were obtained from the AEMPS (February 10th, 2017) and the EMA (September 1st, 2017), respectively. The clinical research ethics committee at Vall d’Hebron Hospital approved this research in March 2020.

Out of 24 eligible patients, we enrolled 20 patients that met inclusion criteria and provided written informed consent. Patients were referred by clinics worldwide based on their refractoriness to previous operative hysteroscopy treatments and provided written consent. The first and last patient inclusions took place on Sept 9th, 2020 and Sept 19th, 2022, respectively. A detailed summary of clinical characteristics of participants pre- and post-treatment is presented in Table 1.

Study outcomes
The primary endpoints of the trial were safety and tolerability of the autologous CD133+ BMDSC therapy by identifying the incidence, prevalence, and frequency of adverse events occurring:
1. During the study period up to 15 months post-treatment.
2. In the event of a term pregnancy
3. In a case of live birth

Secondary endpoints were the efficacy of the therapy in achieving an improvement in morphological and clinical features such as endometrial histology through digital image analysis, endometrial thickness and volume by 2D and 3D vaginal ultrasound, hysteroscopic grading scores (IUAs), menstrual function recorded monthly based on the duration (days), volume (pads/day) and frequency (days) of menstrual bleeding with the Pictorial Blood Assessment Chart13, and reproductive outcomes after treatment measured by pregnancy, miscarriage, ongoing and live birth rates. The interim results of the trial were supervised by an independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) with special focus on the safety data.

Exploratory endpoints included the study of endometrial biopsies before and after stem cell treatment to compare differences in endometrial structure and tissue regeneration mechanisms, as the case of single cell RNA sequencing.

Procedures
Patients were managed as previously described10 with hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) to establish an endometrium with functional equivalence to the proliferative (estrogen dominant) and secretory (progesterone dominant) phases of a normal menstrual cycle before and after stem cell therapy. This was necessary as study patients experienced a lack of regular menstruation or negligible blood loss at menses. During the simulated “secretory phase” (5 days after progesterone administration) pre-treatment and post-treatment endometrial status was monitored by histological digital image analysis, 2D/3D ultrasound (Samsung, South Korea) and hysteroscopic assessment according to ASRM classification of IUAs12 using a 5 mm Betocchi hysteroscope (Karl-Storz, Germany). Hysteroscopic diagnostice valuation was used to grade the severity of AS; however, no operative hysteroscopy was performed. In the four patients for whom images were unavailable, ASRM scoring was verified through direct visualization by both surgeons (X.S. and J.T) during hysteroscopy, with detailed operative notes recorded. Although this represents an unavoidable limitation, we sought to minimize potential bias by applying predefined scoring criteria and maintaining consistent documentation practices.

Endometrial biopsies were performed under hysteroscopic vision from the posterior wall of the uterus at least 1cm away from any visually identified IUA using a semi-rigid double-action biopsy and grasping forceps (Karl-Storz, Germany). The endometrial specimens were processed for histology, ERA26 and EMMA27 to assess endometrial structure, receptivity and microbiome to rule out the existence of dysbiosis, respectively. Single cell RNA seq of biopsies and endometrial organoids were also derived from these endometrial biopsies.

Eligible patients were assessed by the hematology department at Vall Hebron (Barcelona, Spain). Requirements for participation in the study included a patient age of 18–44 years old, a BMI of 18-30, normal liver, heart, and kidney function, the absence of pregnancy, HIV, Hepatitis B or C, syphilis or any psychiatric pathology, and a willingness to complete the study.

BMDSC mobilization was performed using granulocyte-CSF (G-CSF) injection at 10 mcgr/kg for 5 days. CD133+ BMDSCs were collected through peripheral blood apheresis and subsequently isolated. Patients were excluded if they did not reach the minimal requirements for mobilized cells of at least 30 million cells, a purity above 70% and a viability >50%, presented an unstable medical condition, or refused a central venous catheter when required. Isolation of mononuclear cells was then performed by apheresis through peripheral venous access using the CobeSpectra separator (Terumo BCT, Lakewood, CO, USA) according to the manufacturer instructions. Subsequently CD133+ cell selection and isolation were performed using the cell sorter CliniMACS Pro (Miltenyi Biotec GmbH, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany). A mean of 267 min and 2.83 volemias in the apheresis were required to obtain a product with an average viability of a 99.7±0.27% and a mean purity of 89.54±8.29%. The minimum of CD133+ cells to be obtained by selection was 30 million cells that were diluted into 15–30 cc of saline solution and transported in a sterile bag with a syringe to the Interventional Radiology Department at Vall Hebron Hospital for delivery.

Finally, isolated CD133+ BMDSCs were delivered into the spiral arterioles of the patient using a minimal invasive radiology intervention through the left brachial artery, using the Seldinger technique28. The method consisted of placing a 4F introducer into the artery and catheterizing using a 2-curve Cobra angiographic catheter and a 0.035” Terumo guide wire. Through the Cobra catheter, a 2.5F microcatheter with a 0.014” guide wire was inserted and used to catheterize both uterine arteries up to the most distal level allowed by the microcatheter. The procedure was carried out under procedural sedation. Once the catheter was stabilized and its position verified, approximately 15-20 mL containing a mean CD133+ cell dose of 122×10^6±48×10^6 cells (range 42–200×10^6 cells) were administered.

All the diagnostic procedures (2D/3D ultrasound, diagnostic hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsies) before and one month after autologous CD133+ BMDSC administration in an outpatient setting were performed by the same surgeon (X.S.). In the four patients for whom IUAs images were unavailable, ASRM scoring was verified through direct visualization by both surgeons (X.S. and J.T) during hysteroscopy. Afterwards, patients were invited to undergo single embryo transfer (SET). All safety and effectiveness outcomes were recorded during the 15 months following treatment.

Pictorial Blood Assessment Chart (PBAC)
Endometrial function after cell therapy was assessed clinically by the recovery of menstrual function in terms of blood loss with a validated menstrual pictogram7. This method uses a score based on the number and staining of tampons and/or menstrual pads used per menstrual period. Each score number is comparable to a milliliter of blood loss. Menstrual pictograms were provided after the hysteroscopy following stem cell therapy, and the patient was requested to monitor menstrual cycles for six months if any menstrual cycles occurred (See Table 3).

Immunohistochemistry
Endometrial samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde overnight and embedded in paraffin for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining or immunofluorescence. For immunofluorescence, 10 μm-thick paraffin sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating the slides in 10 mM sodium citrate buffer (pH 8-9) at 95–100°C for 20 min, followed by cooling at room temperature for 20 min. Sections were then permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min and blocked for 1 h at room temperature in PBS containing 3% BSA and 0.1% Tween-20. Samples were incubated overnight at 4°C with goat anti-ANGPTL2 primary antibody (R&D Systems, Cat# AF623) or goat anti-SLPI (R&D Systems Cat# AF1274), both diluted 1:100 in blocking buffer. After washing with PBS, sections were incubated for 1 h at room temperature in the dark with donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (Invitrogen, 1:400). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/mL) for 5 min. Slides were mounted with antifade mounting medium and imaged using a Confocal fluorescence microscope Stellaris 5.

Digital image analysis
Endometrial biopsy sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) were digitized with a VENTANA iScan HT slide scanner (Roche) at 20X and analyzed in QuPath29. Samples selected had intact glands and extracellular matrix (ECM), excluding regions with necrosis or hemorrhage. Gland sections from 13 patients (pre- and post-treatment) were carefully segmented using the brush and wand QuPath annotation tools and luminal epithelium was excluded to obtain a specific annotation for the gland epithelium.

Epithelial cell nuclei from the gland were then detected using StarDist, a deep-learning extension script for star-convex nuclear detection based on pre-trained datasets of H&E images (http://github.com/qupath/qupath-extension-stardist). Morphometric data on lumen, gland, and gland epithelium were gathered, calculating lumen percentage within glands and epithelial cell density. Stromal areas were using StarDist and ECM-related features (collagen, ground substance, and vessels) such as ingurgitated vessels and small diffuse hemorrhagic area included were obtained by training a pixel classification-based Artificial Neural Network with full resolution (0.25 μm/px) in QuPath. The resulting classifier corresponding to each ECM component was then applied to all samples and a percentage relative to the stroma area was obtained. Percentage of hematoxylin-stained cell nuclei was obtained by subtracting the area occupied by the ECM components to the stroma annotation. Cases with the existence of ECM underlying the uterine lumen lining epithelium with evidenced stroma decidualization were qualitatively evaluated by an expert pathologist.

Processing and dissociation of endometrial biopsies for single cell analysis
A two-stage dissociation protocol separated endometrial biopsies into stromal fibroblasts and epithelial-enriched single-cell suspensions. Before dissociation, tissue was rinsed with PBS in a petri dish to remove blood and mucus, and excess PBS was removed after rinsing. The tissue was then minced into small pieces and dissociated with 3 mL collagenase mix (Collagenase V, Sigma, USA), RPMI+10% fetal bovine serum, and DNase I (Sigma, USA) at 37°C under continuous shaking at 175 rpm for 25 min in a 15 mL Falcon tube in a horizontal position. This primary enzymatic step mostly dissociates stromal fibroblasts into single cells while leaving epithelial glands and lumen mostly undigested. The contents were transferred to a 50 mL tube in RPMI media and filtered with a 100 μm cell strainer. The tissue remaining on the filter was used for the epithelial enrichment cell isolation by resuspending and incubating in 10 mL Trypsin mix (Trypsin-EDTA (0.25%) phenol and DNase I) for 10 min. The resulting two contents were transferred to 50 mL tubes with 20 mL RPMI, filtered with a 100 μm cell strainer, centrifuged, and then resuspended in 1 mL RPMI. Dead cells were removed using the MACS dead cell removal kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Germany). Live-cell suspensions were loaded into a Chromium Next GEM Chip G (10X Genomics, USA) to obtain cDNA from individual cells.

10x Genomics Chromium library preparation and sequencing
Cells suspension was loaded into a Chromium Next GEM Chip G (10x Genomics) and run in a Chromium Controller (10x Genomics). cDNA synthesis and amplification were performed using the Single Cell 3’ Reagent Kit v3.1 (10x Genomics). 25% of the resulting cDNA was used for enzymatic fragmentation, end repair, A-tailing, adapter ligation, and amplification (with an expected yield of 0.1 ng/μl and a peak size between 200 and 9000 bp as determined in a TapeStation using HSD1000 assay reagents), serving as a quality control. Libraries were then quantified in a TapeStation using HSD1000 assay reagents.

10x-Genomics v3 libraries were prepared as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced, aiming at a minimum coverage of 50,000 raw reads per cell, on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S2 v1.5 300 cycles at a mean 40x coverage (paired-end; read 1: 26 cycles; i7 index: 8 cycles, i5 index: 0 cycles; read 2: 98 cycles).

Alignment and quantification of 10X scRNA-seq data
scRNA-seq data was processed using Cell Ranger v3.1.0 and Seurat v4. These versions were maintained to ensure consistency with a previously analyzed dataset and to enable direct comparability3. While newer versions include improvements in cell calling, UMI correction, doublet detection, and annotation, we applied the same pipeline and stringent quality controls across all samples to minimize technical variability. Core Seurat steps—normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and visualization—also improved across versions. Nevertheless, we consider our biological interpretations robust, while acknowledging possible limitations in sensitivity and cross-study compatibility with newer software releases.

Raw reads were demultiplexed using the mkfastq wrapper command for bcl2fastq (Illumina). Libraries were aligned to the GRCh38-3.0.0 reference genome (based on GRCh38.p12, NCBI: GCA_000001405.27), as provided by 10x Genomics. Gene expression count matrices were generated per sample using the count pipeline with default parameters. This pipeline includes read alignment using the STAR aligner, UMI counting, barcode calling, and filtering of empty droplets. The filtering step relies on a Good-Turing smoothing model of background gene expression to distinguish low-RNA-content cells from ambient RNA.

Quality control filtering of cells and doublet detection
Low-quality cells were filtered out based on quality control metrics. Specifically, cells with a low number of detected genes or a high proportion of mitochondrial reads were excluded. All quality control procedures and downstream analyses were performed using R (v4.1). Doublet detection was performed with two methods: DoubletFinder (v2.0.3) and scds (v1.6.0) packages. The expected doublet formation rate was fixed for each sample according to the cell count recovery given per sample by Cell Ranger. The hybrid approach from the scds package was used to avoid removing false-positive doublets. Cells marked as doublets by both algorithms were removed from the samples.

Integration of scRNA-seq data across different conditions and cell clustering
Individual samples were aggregated, processed, and integrated with functions from the Seurat (v4.0.1) package. First, sample-to-sample aggregation for each condition dataset was performed with the merge function. Next, each aggregated dataset (pre-AS and post-AS therapy) was processed with the SCTransform. The SCTransform pipeline integrates different study conditions by applying a regularized negative binomial regression to allow the detection of condition-to-condition shared cell identities and the performance of differential expression analysis. Mitochondrial ratios and cell cycle phase were regressed out from integrated datasets. The 3000 most variable genes present in combined datasets using the SelectIntegrationFeatures function were used. PrepSCTIntegration and FindIntegrationAnchors were applied to identify the anchoring vectors across datasets and integration steps performed with IntegrateData (normalization method set to SCT). In the dimensional reduction step, the first 30 dimensions of PCA and UMAP were used to visualize cell clusters on the nearest-neighbor graphs. The clustree (0.4.4) package was used to evaluate the optimal resolution number in the FindCluster function; multiple clusters with a range of resolution from 0.5 to 3 were generated, with increased steps of 0.1. A manual review of the generated UMAPs and clustree output determined an optimal resolution of 0.8 to label the different clusters. The integration step was validated by evaluating the conservation of canonical markers across pre- and post-conditions.

Annotation of cell types in scRNA-seq datasets
Cell type identification was conducted by examining the differentially expressed genes of each cluster in comparison to the others. The Wilcoxon Rank Sum test was used, and the p-values were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) method. Cluster cell identity was evaluated by comparison of cluster marker genes that were compared to annotated major cell types reported in published endometrial atlases10,24.

Analysis of significant changes in cell population sizes
Cell ratio analysis across different experimental groups was performed using a pseudobulk strategy. A count matrix of the different cell types detected per sample was created, and the edgeR (v3.34.0) package was used to compute a differential abundance (DA) test across cell types. The FDR p-value adjusting method was applied.

Cell-to-cell communication network analysis
To study the possible signaling interactions between cells, total interaction probabilities and communication information flows were determined with the CellChat (v1.1.3) package23. The first measure indicates the probability of communication between two cell types; the total probability of interaction is split into two parts: the probability of interaction between the sender and receiver and sender cell, considering the number of interactions (ligand-receptor or L-R pairs expressed) and the level of expression (strength of the interaction). A database of 229 families of signaling pathways was used to obtain information regarding interactions; this curated list of molecules considers the known structure of L-R pairs, including multimeric complexes, soluble agonists and antagonists, stimulators, and inhibitory co-receptors. The second measure, the communication information flow, assesses the amount of information exchanged between several cells through various interactions. A higher value of communication information flow between cell populations indicates a more complex communication network. The population.size argument in the computeCommunProb function was used to correct the communication weight of each cell population. The cell-to-cell communication (CCC) networks were filtered to exclude those with fewer than ten cells to achieve robust results. The rankNet function with a significance threshold of 0.05 was used to test for network differences between AS endometrial samples pre- and post-treatment with CD133+ BMDSCs. These comparisons included only common cell types, excluding cycling cells from the analysis. Significantly altered signaling pathways between groups are highlighted in the bar graphs of the flow of information. To explore these plots further, interaction probability scatter plots can be used to identify the receiving and sending cells. The contribution of each L-R pair to a pathway is also shown in interaction probability plots.

MAESTER library preparation, sequencing and analysis
The methodology was applied as previously described14. Briefly, MAESTER consists of two PCRs, whereby we would include 10x Genomics 3’ v3 cDNA from where the CB and UMI of the transcripts would be retained. In the first PCR, twelve primers were used to tile across the whole mitochondrial transcriptome at 1 μM each together with a specific barcode GoT-P5-i5-BCXX for each sample14. The mixture was as follows: 20 μL of KAPA HiFi Hotstart ReadyMix (Thermofisher Scientific), 16 μL of cDNA product, (diluted to achieve at least 1 ng/uL) along with 3 μL of primer mix 10 μM and 1 μL of Got-P5-i5-BCXX (10 μM). The PCR was set to initial denaturation at 95°C for 3 min followed by 10 cycles of 98°C for 20 s, 65°C for 15 s and 72°C for 3 min, with a final extension at 72°C for 5 min. After amplification, each individual primer generated 12 reactions, and so these were pooled together at a ratio of: mix 1: 32 μL; mix 2: 40 μL; mix 3: 40 μL; mix 4: 40 μL; mix 5: 40 μL; mix 6: 40 μL; mix 7: 40 μL; mix 8: 40 μL; mix 9: 8 μL; mix 10: 8 μL; mix 11: 8 μL and mix 12: 16 μL.

The pooled products were purified with 1× AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter, USA) as per protocol instructions. After AMPure XP purification, the pooled PCR 1 product was eluted in 20 μl H2O RNAse free. Thereafter, the PCR 2 was performed by adding 18 μl of the purified product from PCR 1, with 2 μl of a 5 μM primer mix (P5-generic + GoT-P7-i7-BCXX)14 and 20 μl KAPA HiFi Hotstart ReadyMix (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

The parameters used for PCR 2 were an initial denaturation at 95°C for 3 min; six cycles of 98°C for 20 s, 60°C for 30 s and 72°C for 3 min, followed by a final extension at 72°C for 5 min. The resultant PCR was purified with 0.8X AMPure XP beads. The DNA was eluted in 20 μL TE, quantified and sequenced accordingly. The libraries contained 0.6–50 ng/μL with sizes ranging from 300 to 1,500 bp and were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq X 10B sequencing (paired-end; read 1: 28 cycles; read 2: 256 cycles, 2× 8-bp index barcodes).

Raw sequencing data was pre-processed according to the pipeline previously described14, up to the generation of BAM files containing mitochondrial reads from individual cells in the respective scRNA-Seq samples. An additional preprocessing step was implemented to trim 50 nucleotides from the 3’ ends and remove poly-A tails, using Fastp v0.23.430. Then, BAM files were split by cell barcodes, and each subset was processed independently. Duplicated reads were removed using fgbio v2.1.0 (fulcrumgenomics/fgbio: 2.4.0 (2.4.0)). To exclude low-quality cells, the total number of covered bases per cell was calculated using samtools v1.19.231 and bedtools v2.31.132. Only cells with coverage exceeding the overall median minus one standard deviation were retained for downstream analyses. Variant calling was performed with LoFreq v2.1.533 following base recalibration, which was conducted using the GATK toolkit v4.5.0.034 (DePristo, 2011) and LoFreq. The resulting VCF files were normalized using bcftools v1.1831 and filtered. Selected variants included those detected in the CD133 population of the CD133 samples and shared with S2/E2 samples while excluding variants identified in S1/E1 samples. Additionally, variants were retained only if they exhibited a variant allele frequency exceeding 10% per cell and were detected in at least five cells, but excluded if present in ≥90% of total cells. Filtered variants were manually reviewed using IGV v2.12.335. Variants with more than 10 reads in S1/E1 were discarded. The final set of variants was added to the metadata of the scRNA-seq objects using the Seurat (v5.1.0) package36 in R v4.2.2.

Differential expression and gene signatures score
The FindMarkers function from the Seurat package was used to perform differential expression analysis across the treatment stages and the different cell types reported in the dataset. The Wilcoxon Rank Sum test was used, and the p-values were corrected using the FDR method. Genes with FDR values under 0.05 were considered significant. Gene set signature scoring was performed using escape (v1.6.0) package37 and UCell package to study menstrual cycle function in the secretory phase between treatment groups. The AddModuleScore function from UCell package was used to compute the score for each cell present in the dataset. Finally, the scored differences between treatment stages in the endothelium, epithelium, AS epithelium, perivascular (PV), and stromal cell fractions were evaluated. The getSignificance function was used to perform statistical testing using a Wilcoxon test; p-values were corrected using the FDR method. The following gene set related to menstrual cycle function in the secretory phase was used38: SCGB1D2, MT1F, MT1X, MT1E, MT1G, CXCL14, WNT5A, SFRP1, ZFYVE21, CILP, SLF2, MATN2, and S100A4.

Organoid culture from endometrial biopsies
Organoids were generated from AS patients’ endometrium pre- and post-treatment and from healthy control endometrium. After enzymatic dissociation of the endometrial biopsies, epithelial and stromal cells were obtained and total cell numbers were counted. After centrifugation at 300g, the pellet was resuspended in 70% Matrigel (Corning, 356231) and 30% DMEM/F12 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11330032) and supplemented with the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (1/500). The suspension was cultured in 20-μL droplets containing 25,000 cells, deposited in prewarmed 48-well plates, and allowed to form a gel at 37°C and 5% CO2 before adding culture medium. Organoid culture medium was prepared as previously described39,40. Matrigel droplets were cultured for 14-16 days in the first passage (P0) with medium changes every two days. Organoids were then grown for seven days before the following passage, with media changes every two days.

Organoids were recovered for passaging by liquifying the Matrigel droplets with ice-cold DMEM/F12 (without any growth factors, serum, or enzymes), followed by repeated pipetting to ensure maximum recovery. Organoids were then dissociated by incubation with TrypLE supplemented with Y-27632 (1/1000) and mechanically triturated. The resulting cell suspension was centrifuged at 300g, and the pellets were resuspended in 70% Matrigel and 30% DMEM/F12 supplemented with Y-27632 and placed as droplets in 48-well plates. Two passages were performed to remove the contaminating stromal cells from the epithelial organoids. After seven days of P2 culture, organoids were dissociated for single-cell transcriptomic analysis following the same protocol described for passaging but with an additional cell counting step for the single-cell transcriptomics protocol as per manufacturer’s instructions (10x Genomics).

Organoid counting
Multiple microscopy images (Thermo Fisher, EVOS M5000) were taken to count organoids present in each Matrigel droplet. Images were taken by dividing each drop into two depth sections and each section into four regions. Two images were counted diagonally from each section, and the mean from these images was calculated. This mean was multiplied by the number of divisions of each section (4) and the number of sections (2) to infer the total organoid number per drop. For each condition, two experimental replicates were measured. For organoid counting we conducted a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Tukey’s HSD post-hoc tests to assess pairwise comparisons between the control, CD133+ BMDSC pre-treatment and post-treatment AS EEOs per passage.

Organoids scRNA-seq
Single-cell RNA-seq data from organoids were aggregated, processed, and integrated using a similar approach to that described for the patient-derived samples. Briefly, integration across pre-treatment, post-treatment, and control datasets was performed using the SCTransform function. Dimensionality reduction was conducted based on the 750 most highly variable genes using the first 30 principal components, and cell clusters were visualized using UMAP on the nearest-neighbor graph. Finally, major cell types were identified and annotated by analyzing differentially expressed genes in each cluster, using previously described cell-type-specific marker genes10,24.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis of clinical design. The study sample size was estimated based on the hypothesis that autologous CD133+ BMDSCs instillation in the uterine arteries improves endometrial function in terms of reproductive outcomes, specifically live birth (LB) rate. It was designed as a paired cohort study “before and after”, consisting of the same patient undergoing embryo transfer after treatment. Our hypothesis was that improvement would involve a transition from 0% prior to stem cell treatment to 28% LB rate after treatment (α 0.05, power=80%) which is the average LB rate reported in the context of assisted reproduction treatments by the European IVF-Monitoring Consortium41. Based on these assumptions, it was estimated that 18 patients would be required for the protocol study. Additionally, a 20% loss to follow-up was anticipated, resulting in a required total of 20 patients. The final analysis was conducted after all patients completed a 15-month follow-up after treatment. However, since the actual drop-out rate was much lower than expected (only 5%), we successfully completed 19 per protocol patients out of 20 recruited, surpassing our pre-specified target of 18 per protocol patients. Given that recruiting patients with this rare condition was challenging, and upon consultation and agreement with our Ethics Committee, we concluded recruitment once the necessary number of patients had been successfully treated and completed follow-up.

Statistical analysis of clinical outcomes. For the secondary endpoints, a convenience sample was studied. Endometrial volume, thickness, IUA score from Figs. 2, 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1B, C was presented as mean±standard deviation. Statistical significance between endometrial volume and thickness was evaluated using a parametric paired t-test. Normality assumption was confirmed by applying the Shapiro–Wilk test to assess the distribution of differences between pre and post treatment for each parameter. For the IUA score, non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test was applied.

Data from digital analyses presented in Supplementary Fig. 1A is presented as mean±standard error of the mean (S.E.M). Statistical significance between general characteristics of gland and stroma in paired samples grouped based on reproductive outcomes was evaluated using a parametric paired t-test whereas differences between specific characteristics of gland and stroma were assessed using a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Statistical significance within pre- and post-AS therapy between these groups was evaluated using non-parametrical Kruskal Wallis with Dunn’s test for multiple comparisons.

Statistical significance was considered when the p-value was less than 0.05 and was indicated as follows: p<0.05 (*), p<0.01 (**), p<0.005 (***), and p<0.0001 (****). Data was analyzed and represented using GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 and 10.2.0 software.

Statistical analysis for single cell data of in vivo biopsies. Statistical analyses were performed in software R (v4.1 and v4.2, https://www.r-project.org). Data from Fig. 4B, displaying boxplots of gene signature enrichment scores (UCellScore), were statistically tested using the Wilcoxon test implemented via the getSignificance function from the escape (v1.6.0) package. P-values were adjusted using the FDR correction method.

Data from Fig. 4C, showing cell type ratios boxplots, were analyzed using a negative binomial generalized linear model (NB-GLM) implemented in the edgeR (v3.34.0) package. Statistical significance was defined as FDR<0.05 (**), and FDR<0.1 (*).

For the data shown in Fig. 4D, we conducted a differential CCC analysis between pre-treatment (Pre-AS therapy) and post-treatment (Post-AS therapy) samples using the rankNet function from the CellChat (v1.1.3) package. Statistical significance was assessed with a Wilcoxon test, applying a significance threshold of 0.001 and a p-value cutoff of 0.01. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the FDR correction method.

Data from Supplementary Fig. 3, displaying dot plots of the differential expression between Pre-AS therapy and Post-AS therapy across different cell types, were statistically tested using the Wilcoxon test implemented via the findMarkers function from the Seurat (v4.0.1) package, with p-values corrected for multiple comparisons using the FDR method.

Supplementary Fig. 4, showing cellular communication through chord plots and bar plots, was generated using the netVisual_aggregate and netAnalysis_contribution functions from the CellChat (v1.1.3) package, respectively. A p-value threshold of 0.05 was applied to define significant interactions and contributions.

Statistical analysis for organoids. For organoid counting we conducted a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Tukey’s HSD post-hoc tests to assess pairwise comparisons between the groups. Data was analyzed and represented using GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 and 10.2.0 software.

### Reviewer 4

Comments on “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial” As requested by the Editor, our review will be limited to those aspects that relate to the trial design and statistics of this manuscript. We do not have sufficient experience and knowledge for evaluation of aspects that are more specific to cells and laboratory work. Considering that Asherman Syndrome has a significant impact on the quality of life of many people, and that currently the only possible intervention - which is often not definitive - is operative hysteroscopy, the identification of different approaches could be of great value. This is especially true if these possible new interventions are able to overcome infertility. Therefore, we commend the authors for their commitment to the search for new treatment options. We thus appreciated the authors’ effort in conducting this clinical trial aimed at evaluating the tolerability, safety, and efficacy of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy in patients with Asherman Syndrome (AS) refractory to surgical interventions. Overall, the methodological components of the study are appropriate for a non-randomised, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. We are of the opinion that the study design is well-structured, and we do not have any major comments on this aspect. However, considering that the study represents a complex methodological project integrating clinical and molecular approaches, we believe that some clarifications and further details may be useful, both regarding the objectives of the study and the use of statistics. This is all the more important given that the sample consisted of 20 women (one of whom did not complete the study), which is relatively large considering the prevalence of the disease, but relatively small considering the numerous endpoints set by the authors. We reiterate the importance of this study and offer some comments and suggestions to further improve the clarity, transparency and robustness of the analyses. Major comments 1. Partially addressed primary endpoints According to the trial registration on the European Union Clinical Trial Register (EudraCT: 2016-003975-23), three primary endpoints were declared: “1. Identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur in the patient throughout the study up until Month 15 post-treatment. 2. In the event of a term pregnancy, identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur during the pregnancy, birth and puerperal period. 3. In case of a Live Birth (LB), identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events that may be associated with the investigational medicinal product (IMP) until the first month of age.” However, in the present study, only the first primary endpoint appears to have been thoroughly developed, and its results reported. The results of the primary endpoints are reported in the manuscript on lines 109-116 and in Table 2. There is no mention of primary endpoints 2 and 3, i.e. pregnancies and births. Some information on these is provided in secondary endpoints section and in the supplementary material, but as these are primary endpoints - and therefore theoretically the most important ones - they should be clearly presented in the section of the results dealing with the primary endpoints. It would be appropriate for the authors to complete the analysis by including the remaining two primary endpoints as outlined in the registered protocol. Alternatively, the authors should state why the results of the other two primary endpoints were not reported in the primary endpoint results section and were not discussed. For example, the most outstanding result of this study is mentioned by the authors in the abstract: "...reproductive function was restored, culminating in six live births after embryo transfer". It is not clear why this striking observation is barely mentioned in the manuscript, neither in the results nor in the discussion, even if one of the primary endpoints was the “identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events” in case of a life birth. It is clear that the set of secondary and explanatory outcomes is intended to try to understand the biological and molecular reasons behind the regained fertility of some women. Nevertheless, the primary endpoint is in danger of being obscured by all the other analyses. 2. Excessive detailing of secondary and exploratory endpoints Although the presentation of the results and discussion of the secondary and exploratory endpoints is comprehensive and thorough, the length and level of detail may be reconsidered as it seems disproportionate to the primary objectives of the study. A more concise approach could benefit the overall focus and readability of the manuscript. Alternatively, the endpoints of the study could be refocused. 3. Predictive model based on Support Vector Machine (SVM) In the section concerning endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs), the authors add the use of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) with a kernel radial basis functon(RBF), implemented via the scPred package, to perform transcriptomic comparison with in vivo data. However, although a brief description of the process is provided (10-fold cross-validation and C parameter optimization), several key methodological elements are missing, e.g. the type of learning adopted, the target classes used for model training, the feature selection procedure, the model performance metrics, and the rationale for choosing the RBF kernel, among others. Given the complexity and methodological significance of a machine learning-based analysis, we recommend that a dedicated and detailed methods section be added. Alternatively, since this does not represent one of the study’s primary endpoints, the analysis could be considered for omission. Minor comments 1. Statistical methodology presentation Although the statistical methodology covers a broad range of analyses, it is overall unclear, dispersed, and difficult to follow. The statistical tests used are reported in different sections of the methodology and not always in a systematic manner, making it challenging to obtain a comprehensive view of the analyses performed. We therefore recommend including a more structured and concise section that clearly summarizes all the applied tests, the type of data analysed, and the rationale behind the choice of each statistical test. Alternatively, we suggest including a subsection on the statistics and software used within each section of the methodology. This will allow the reader to better understand the different statistical approaches used. 2. Assumptions behind the use of parametric tests When parametric tests were used instead of non-parametric ones, it is not specified whether the assumption of normality of the data distribution was verified. An example of this is the use of the paired t-test to evaluate the IUA score. Since this is a score, it is likely that nonparametric tests would be more appropriate. Or, if a parametric test is needed, it would be appropriate to state the rationale for such a choice. 3. Choice of statistical test for organoid quantification A two-way ANOVA test was used in the organoid quantification section. It would be useful for the authors to clarify the rationale for using a two-way analysis. A two-way ANOVA analyses the effect of two different categorical independent variables on a continuous dependent variable. It is not clear what the two independent variables are in this case. In addition, it is important to specify whether there were two independent interacting factors. Could it be that a one-way ANOVA would have been more appropriate? 4. Statistical power and sample size calculation The authors calculated the sample size based on a hypothetical increase in live births from 0% to 28%. The hypothesis is probably correct. However, this sample size calculation assumes that the primary objective of the trial is to examine the percentage of women who have a pregnancy that ends in a live birth. For all the other analyses that have been performed, namely those related to secondary and exploratory endpoints, this sample calculation is not as crucial. To give just one example, when it comes to endometrial volume or thickness a sample calculation based on the proportion of life births has no reason to be (even if it is still a paired cohort study). It is sufficient to say that a convenience sample was studied, or the sample size should be computed on a hypothetical difference on volumes or thickness. In any case, in the description of the sample size calculation, the authors do not report the statistical power value used for the estimate. It is recommended that the power and alpha values assumed in the calculation are explicitly reported. 5. Typographical errors. Finally, we suggest a review of, e.g. in the methods section: “Patients were managed as described previously described…”

### Reviewer 6

General This phase 1/2 trial assessed the safety, efficacy, and biological plausibility of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy for treating moderate to severe Asherman Syndrome (AS) in 20 infertile women unresponsive to prior treatments. The therapy was well-tolerated, with reversible limb paresthesia as the most common side effect. Significant improvements were observed in endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. Clinically, menstruation and reproductive function were restored, leading to six live births following embryo transfer. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed partial reversion of AS-related changes, and mitochondrial variant tracking showed insights into stem cell engraftment. The results suggest this therapy is safe and effective, warranting further investigation in larger trials. The manuscript is well-written, grammatically sound, and addresses a highly interesting topic, combining stem cell applications as orphan drugs with single-cell technologies. However, some technical aspects related to the bioinformatics analyses, such as the use of older packages (CellRanger, Seurat), as well as the provision of analysis scripts, could benefit from refinement. Major 1. How was the concentration of mobilized cells (at least 30 million cells with >70% purity and >50% viability) determined for this study? Is this concentration commonly used for CD133+ BMDSCs in this application? In cardiac regeneration studies, similar cell collections often use lower concentrations, how does this compare to your approach? 2. Could you explain the rationale behind using CellRanger Software version 3.1.0 (from July 2019) for this analysis, given that the current version is 9.0.1? Additionally, I noticed that Seurat version 4 was used, whereas version 5 is available for quite some time. The use of these older versions, both for CellRanger and Seurat, can potentially result in different analysis outcomes due to improvements or changes in data processing and downstream analysis methods introduced in newer versions. 3. Did the authors also perform quality assessments using tools like MultiQC to aggregate the overall quality of the samples? It might be beneficial to provide these quality reports as supplemental material to account for the sequencing quality. 4. Did the authors also perform dataset integration using Harmony (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0619-0) in addition to the SCT transformation, which is commonly considered a standard approach for handling batch effects, particularly when samples have been processed in different batches? While Harmony is mentioned in the methods section, it appears to be described within the machine learning part, rather than in the single-cell processing section. Could you clarify when Harmony was applied in the analysis and why it was not used in all experiments? 5. Could you please include the cell-to-cell communication analyses in the methods section? 6. Providing the relevant scripts in a public repository would greatly enhance the overall reproducibility and depths of the data analysis. Minor 1. The required number of patients is inconsistent between the methods section and the study protocol, 20 versus 22. It may be helpful for the authors and readers to standardize and use a single number throughout the entire work. 2. The authors also may provide the exact version of the genome build used GRCh38-3.0.0. 3. Did the authors used specific databases, tools or scientific literature to annotate the single cell clusters - Reference 3 in the main manuscript (results) might be added also in the methods section in more detail, if the annotation is mainly based on previous works of the authors, including the species under investigation (e.g., murine, cell-based, …). 4. How was the selection of the 9 out of 20 patients was conducted for the single-cell analysis? 5. Please remove the “.” In the middle of the sentence in line 327.

Moreover, as previously stated, the autologous nature of the therapy significantly limits the ability to detect engraftment events and to establish quantitative correlations with clinical endpoints. From a bioinformatic perspective, we acknowledge that it is not possible to definitively exclude the possibility that the mitochondrial DNA detected in recipient cells originated from transfer mechanisms. However, we applied stringent thresholds for variant calling, including only high-confidence heteroplasmic variants that were absent in pre-treatment samples and uniquely observed post-treatment, thereby strengthening the specificity of our lineage detection. Miller et al. It's not clear how pericytes are involved in endometrium but in CNS it's very well accepted that pericytes forms the scar tissue after injury and inhibits regeneration. We thank the reviewer for highlighting the relevance of the observed changes in perivascular cells and macrophages following treatment. While it is true that in the central nervous system (CNS), pericytes have been implicated in scar formation and inhibition of regeneration after injury, the role of perivascular cells in the endometrium is distinct and context-dependent. Our data demonstrate a tendency towards increase post-treatment in perivascular cells (putative pericytes), along with a marked reduction in macrophage abundance within the endometrial tissue. In contrast to the central nervous system (CNS), where pericytes have been implicated in the formation of fibrotic scar tissue that hinders regeneration after injury, pericytes in the endometrial context appear to play a distinct, pro-regenerative role. Specifically, endometrial pericytes have been associated with microvascular stability, paracrine support of angiogenesis, and interactions with endothelial and epithelial cells that contribute to cyclical regeneration of the uterine lining (Li et al., 2019). Moreover, perivascular cells in the uterus may also exhibit mesenchymal stem cell-like properties, supporting tissue repair and remodeling rather than fibrotic encapsulation (Spitzer et al., 2012). The expansion of this population post-treatment may thus reflect the activation of a regenerative niche rather than a fibrotic or inhibitory microenvironment. This is consistent with previous reports in reproductive biology suggesting that perivascular stromal cells coordinate angiogenesis and modulate immune responses during endometrial regeneration (Gargett et al., 2016). In parallel, the observed reduction in macrophage abundance—particularly those associated with inflammatory phenotypes—suggests a shift away from active inflammation toward immune resolution and tissue remodeling. This dynamic is similar to processes described in successful tissue repair across organ systems, where a timely reduction of pro-inflammatory macrophages, coupled with increased vascular support and stromal cell activation, marks a transition toward functional healing (Davies et al., 2013). These findings have now been further elaborated in the revised Discussion to clarify the functional implications of the cellular changes we observed and to distinguish the uterine regenerative context from that of CNS injury and scarring. Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): Comments on “Autologous cell therapy with CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cells for Asherman Syndrome: a phase 1/2 trial” As requested by the Editor, our review will be limited to those aspects that relate to the trial design and statistics of this manuscript. We do not have sufficient experience and knowledge for evaluation of aspects that are more specific to cells and laboratory work. Considering that Asherman Syndrome has a significant impact on the quality of life of many people, and that currently the only possible intervention - which is often not definitive - is operative hysteroscopy, the identification of different approaches could be of great value. This is especially true if these possible new interventions are able to overcome infertility. Therefore, we commend the authors for their commitment to the search for new treatment options. We thus appreciated the authors’ effort in conducting this clinical trial aimed at evaluating the tolerability, safety, and efficacy of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy in patients with Asherman Syndrome (AS) refractory to surgical interventions. Overall, the methodological components of the study are appropriate for a non-randomised, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. We are of the opinion that the study design is well-structured, and we do not have any major comments on this aspect. However, considering that the study represents a complex methodological project integrating clinical and molecular approaches, we believe that some clarifications and further details may be useful, both regarding the objectives of the study and the use of statistics. This is all the more important given that the sample consisted of 20 women (one of whom did not complete the study), which is relatively large considering the prevalence of the disease, but relatively small considering the numerous endpoints set by the authors. We reiterate the importance of this study and offer some comments and suggestions to further improve the clarity, transparency and robustness of the analyses. A. We sincerely thank Reviewer #4 for the thoughtful and constructive comments, as well as the recognition of the importance of our study and the efforts made by our multidisciplinary team over the past four years. We are especially grateful for your acknowledgment of the significance of developing new therapeutic strategies for Asherman Syndrome (AS), a condition with considerable impact on patients' quality of life and limited treatment options. We appreciate your positive assessment of the trial design and the methodological framework of our non-randomized, open-label, single-arm, phase 1/2 study. Your recognition that the overall structure is appropriate and well-conceived is encouraging and greatly valued. We also acknowledge your suggestion that, given the complexity of our integrated clinical and molecular approach, additional clarifications and details regarding the study objectives and statistical analyses would enhance transparency and rigor—particularly in light of our sample size and the multiple endpoints assessed. We fully agree with this observation and have revised the manuscript accordingly to provide the following: 1. Clarified Study Objectives: We have updated the Methods section to explicitly distinguish between primary, secondary and exploratory objectives (lines 22-41) 2. Statistical Considerations: We have rewritten the statistical section part to include more details on how each analysis was performed as further described below. We hope that these revisions address your concerns and contribute to a more transparent and robust presentation of our findings. Once again, we thank you for your expert evaluation and for your helpful suggestions to improve our manuscript. Major comments 1. Partially addressed primary endpoints According to the trial registration on the European Union Clinical Trial Register (EudraCT: 2016-003975-23), three primary endpoints were declared: “1. Identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur in the patient throughout the study up until Month 15 post-treatment. 2. In the event of a term pregnancy, identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of different adverse events that may occur during the pregnancy, birth and puerperal period. 3. In case of a Live Birth (LB), identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events that may be associated with the investigational medicinal product (IMP) until the first month of age.” However, in the present study, only the first primary endpoint appears to have been thoroughly developed, and its results reported. The results of the primary endpoints are reported in the manuscript on lines 109-116 and in Table 2. There is no mention of primary endpoints 2 and 3, i.e. pregnancies and births. Some information on these is provided in secondary endpoints section and in the supplementary material, but as these are primary endpoints - and therefore theoretically the most important ones - they should be clearly presented in the section of the results dealing with the primary endpoints. It would be appropriate for the authors to complete the analysis by including the remaining two primary endpoints as outlined in the registered protocol. Alternatively, the authors should state why the results of the other two primary endpoints were not reported in the primary endpoint results section and were not discussed. For example, the most outstanding result of this study is mentioned by the authors in the abstract: "...reproductive function was restored, culminating in six live births after embryo transfer". It is not clear why this striking observation is barely mentioned in the manuscript, neither in the results nor in the discussion, even if one of the primary endpoints was the “identification of incidence, prevalence and frequency of the different adverse events” in case of a life birth. It is clear that the set of secondary and explanatory outcomes is intended to try to understand the biological and molecular reasons behind the regained fertility of some women. Nevertheless, the primary endpoint is in danger of being obscured by all the other analyses. A1. Thank you for your insightful analysis of the trial design. As noted by the reviewer, we have now provided further information of the incidence, prevalence, and frequency of various adverse events that may occur: These endpoints are now outlined in the section “primary endpoints” in lines 112-129. We have also added further explanation in the discussion (line 338-344). 2. Excessive detailing of secondary and exploratory endpoints Although the presentation of the results and discussion of the secondary and exploratory endpoints is comprehensive and thorough, the length and level of detail may be reconsidered as it seems disproportionate to the primary objectives of the study. A more concise approach could benefit the overall focus and readability of the manuscript. Alternatively, the endpoints of the study could be refocused. A2. Thank you for your comments. We have made every effort to be concise in our presentation of secondary and exploratory endpoints. However, the amount of information extracted from the exploratory (scRNA-seq) analysis to describe the molecular mechanisms of the therapy is very large and even if we have shortened it, it still requires a significant space in the manuscript. Additionally, other reviewers have requested to further emphasize into these findings, so we have had to extend certain parts of this analysis. Besides, it is important to consider the breadth of clinical, biological, and basic research that supports not only the effectiveness but also the mechanism of action of this therapy. Nonetheless, since we have now added more information about the primary end points, we believe there is now a more balanced structure between the primary and secondary/exploratory end points. 3. Predictive model based on Support Vector Machine (SVM) In the section concerning endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs), the authors add the use of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) with a kernel radial basis functon(RBF), implemented via the scPred package, to perform transcriptomic comparison with in vivo data. However, although a brief description of the process is provided (10-fold cross-validation and C parameter optimization), several key methodological elements are missing, e.g. the type of learning adopted, the target classes used for model training, the feature selection procedure, the model performance metrics, and the rationale for choosing the RBF kernel, among others. Given the complexity and methodological significance of a machine learning-based analysis, we recommend that a dedicated and detailed methods section be added. Alternatively, since this does not represent one of the study’s primary endpoints, the analysis could be considered for omission. A3. As the reviewer correctly notes, this analysis does not represent a primary endpoint of the study and may potentially confuse readers when interpreting the organoid results. Therefore, we have decided to omit it and it has been now removed from Figure 5 and methods section. Minor comments 1. Statistical methodology presentation Although the statistical methodology covers a broad range of analyses, it is overall unclear, dispersed, and difficult to follow. The statistical tests used are reported in different sections of the methodology and not always in a systematic manner, making it challenging to obtain a comprehensive view of the analyses performed. We therefore recommend including a more structured and concise section that clearly summarizes all the applied tests, the type of data analysed, and the rationale behind the choice of each statistical test. Alternatively, we suggest including a subsection on the statistics and software used within each section of the methodology. This will allow the reader to better understand the different statistical approaches used. A1. Thank you for your valuable comment. We have now structured the statistical section into various parts: Statistical analysis of clinical design and data outcomes, statistical analysis for single cell data of in vivo biopsies and statistical analysis for organoids. We believe this organization makes the statistical tests easier to access and understand. 2. Assumptions behind the use of parametric tests When parametric tests were used instead of non-parametric ones, it is not specified whether the assumption of normality of the data distribution was verified. An example of this is the use of the paired t-test to evaluate the IUA score. Since this is a score, it is likely that nonparametric tests would be more appropriate. Or, if a parametric test is needed, it would be appropriate to state the rationale for such a choice. A2. Thank you very much for this helpful comment. We have now updated the Statistical Analysis section to include the normality assessments, which had been omitted in the previous version. Specifically, we used the Shapiro–Wilk test to evaluate the normality assumption for each dataset. Regarding the use of parametric tests in Figures 2 and 3 (endometrial volume, thickness, and IUA score), we initially selected the paired t-test because the data consist of paired measurements from the same patients before and after treatment, and when normality is satisfied, parametric tests provide greater statistical power. To ensure this approach was appropriate, we tested each dataset for normality. For endometrial volume and thickness, the data met the normality assumption and thus justified the use of the paired t-test. However, for the IUA score shown in Figure 4, you are absolutely right—normality was only observed in the post-treatment data. Therefore, we additionally applied the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which yielded the same statistical significance as the paired t-test (p < 0.0001). We agree this is a more appropriate approach, and we have accordingly updated both the graph and the statistical test presented. Just to double check, we did perform now both parametric and non-parametric tests to verify robustness of results and ensure significance for both scenarios. 3. Choice of statistical test for organoid quantification A two-way ANOVA test was used in the organoid quantification section. It would be useful for the authors to clarify the rationale for using a two-way analysis. A two-way ANOVA analyses the effect of two different categorical independent variables on a continuous dependent variable. It is not clear what the two independent variables are in this case. In addition, it is important to specify whether there were two independent interacting factors. Could it be that a one-way ANOVA would have been more appropriate? A3. We employed a two-way ANOVA for organoid quantification to evaluate the effects of two independent categorical variables: (1) experimental group (AS-Pre EEO, AS-Post EEO, and Control EEO) and (2) passage number (P0, P1, P2), on the continuous dependent variable—organoid count. This analysis allowed us to assess both the main effects of group and passage, as well as their interaction, indicating whether the treatment effect varied across passages. This is particularly relevant given that organoids are cultured in a cocktail of growth factors, and repeated passaging may diminish therapeutic effects. The two-way ANOVA thus captured both group differences and passage-dependent dynamics. 4. However, this sample size calculation assumes that the primary objective of the trial is to examine the percentage of women who have a pregnancy that ends in a live birth. For all the other analyses that have been performed, namely those related to secondary and exploratory endpoints, this sample calculation is not as crucial. To give just one example, when it comes to endometrial volume or thickness a sample calculation based on the proportion of life births has no reason to be (even if it is still a paired cohort study). It is sufficient to say that a convenience sample was studied, or the sample size should be computed on a hypothetical difference on volumes or thickness. A4. Thank you for this thoughtful observation. We agree that the original sample size calculation, which was based on an expected increase in live birth rates, primarily supports the trial’s primary objective related to reproductive outcomes. For analyses related to secondary and exploratory endpoints—such as endometrial volume and thickness—we acknowledge that this calculation is not directly applicable. As suggested, we have now clarified in methods section (section Statistical analysis of clinical outcomes) that a convenience sample was used for these secondary analyses. In any case, in the description of the sample size calculation, the authors do not report the statistical power value used for the estimate. It is recommended that the power and alpha values assumed in the calculation are explicitly reported. A4. Thank you for the comment. We have now added the alpha level and statistical power to the Methods section (line 369 of the methods doc inside the subsection of “statistical analysis of clinical design”). Below are the main inputs used for the sample size calculation: • Proportion of events: Group 0 = 0.00% Group 1 = 28.00% • Minimum expected effect size: 28.00% difference • Alpha risk (Type I error): 5% • Power (1 - Type II error): 80% • Test type: One-sided • Expected dropout rate: 20% • Required sample size per group (before dropout adjustment): 18 • Adjusted sample size per group (accounting for 20% dropout): 22 5. Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author): General This phase 1/2 trial assessed the safety, efficacy, and biological plausibility of autologous CD133+ bone marrow-derived stem cell (BMDSC) therapy for treating moderate to severe Asherman Syndrome (AS) in 20 infertile women unresponsive to prior treatments. The therapy was well-tolerated, with reversible limb paresthesia as the most common side effect. Significant improvements were observed in endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. Clinically, menstruation and reproductive function were restored, leading to six live births following embryo transfer. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed partial reversion of AS-related changes, and mitochondrial variant tracking showed insights into stem cell engraftment. The results suggest this therapy is safe and effective, warranting further investigation in larger trials. The manuscript is well-written, grammatically sound, and addresses a highly interesting topic, combining stem cell applications as orphan drugs with single-cell technologies. However, some technical aspects related to the bioinformatics analyses, such as the use of older packages (CellRanger, Seurat), as well as the provision of analysis scripts, could benefit from refinement. Major 1. How was the concentration of mobilized cells (at least 30 million cells with >70% purity and >50% viability) determined for this study? Is this concentration commonly used for CD133+ BMDSCs in this application? In cardiac regeneration studies, similar cell collections often use lower concentrations, how does this compare to your approach? A1. Thank you for this insightful comment. The product specification for the cell therapy—including a minimum of ≥30 million CD133⁺ cells with ≥70% purity and ≥50% viability—was established in agreement with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) during the clinical trial authorization process. As this was a Phase 1–2 trial, these criteria were designed to ensure feasibility, safety, and consistency of the product while allowing for some variability in early-stage manufacturing. Importantly, the cell dose was not arbitrarily selected but was determined by the number of CD133⁺ cells that could be realistically mobilized and recovered from each patient following G-CSF stimulation and apheresis. The threshold of 30 million cells reflected the minimum yield considered necessary for therapeutic delivery, based on preclinical work and prior experience with autologous stem cell therapies. It also accounted for the variability in mobilization capacity across patients. While some cardiac regeneration trials have used lower cell doses, the biological context and clinical indications differ significantly. Cardiac patients typically face life-threatening conditions and are often older, with reduced bone marrow stem cell mobilization capacity. In contrast, our study population comprises younger individuals who are not affected by life-threatening diseases—this is an explicit exclusion criterion of our trial.Therefore, despite administering only minimal doses of filgrastim, our patients generally exhibit higher cell yields. This enhanced mobilization capacity allows for a more robust collection of CD133+ cells. Importantly, this Phase I/II trial was designed to determine the optimal therapeutic dosage. In line with this objective—and owing to the biological advantages mentioned—it is expected that higher cell dosages will be obtained. Our primary goal was to ensure the administration of a therapeutically relevant cell dose, while simultaneously maintaining patient safety and manufacturing feasibility. 2. Could you explain the rationale behind using CellRanger Software version 3.1.0 (from July 2019) for this analysis, given that the current version is 9.0.1? Additionally, I noticed that Seurat version 4 was used, whereas version 5 is available for quite some time. The use of these older versions, both for CellRanger and Seurat, can potentially result in different analysis outcomes due to improvements or changes in data processing and downstream analysis methods introduced in newer versions. The rationale behind using CellRanger v3.1.0 (released July 2019) and Seurat v4 lies in the study’s timeline. The experimental protocol was approved and initiated on April 20, 2020, at which point CellRanger v3.1.0 and Seurat v4 were the most stable and supported versions for our pipeline. Importantly, re-analysis with newer versions would introduce inconsistencies between the original pipeline and current computational standards, potentially affecting reproducibility and interpretation. We also note that CellRanger v3.1.0 was last updated in February 2025 for archival maintenance, and Seurat v4 remained the working version throughout our analysis pipeline, even though v5 has been available since November 2023. While newer versions offer improvements, the results and conclusions of this study remain robust and directly comparable within the analytical context under which they were originally generated and published (Santamaria, X., Roson, B., Perez-Moraga, R. et al., Decoding the endometrial niche of Asherman’s Syndrome at single-cell resolution, Nat Commun 14, 5890 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41656-1) 3. Did the authors also perform quality assessments using tools like MultiQC to aggregate the overall quality of the samples? It might be beneficial to provide these quality reports as supplemental material to account for the sequencing quality. A3. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding MultiQC. Unfortunately, integrating MultiQC is not feasible in this context because the version of CellRanger (3.1.0) used in our study is not fully compatible with MultiQC’s current parsers. Therefore, we provide individual per-sample QC reports generated by CellRanger, which accurately reflect the quality of the data generated using our original pipeline. Nat Com 2023) and the current analysis. Therefore, to maintain coherence across studies, we retained the original SCT-based integration for downstream analyses. 5. The rationale for performing stem cell treatment in mid-secretory phase is because progesterone essentially creates a “fertile ground” for the stem cells to recognize, adhere, engraft, and contribute to regeneration. Progesterone transforms the estrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory, receptive state. This includes decidualization of stromal fibroblasts, increased extracellular matrix deposition, and altered immune tolerance. Also, P4 upregulates angiogenic factors such as VEGF and angiopoietins, which make the microvasculature more permeable to circulating cells. In this primed environment, progesterone also induces expression of key chemotactic and adhesion molecules—including CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins—that are critical for guiding stem cells toward the endometrial tissue. Finally, P induces expression of factors like CXCL12 (SDF-1), ICAM-1, and selectins, which guide stem cells toward the endometrial tissue (1-9). Stem cells administered via intravascular injection in uterine microcirculation can reach the spiral arterioles and venules of the endometrium. They express surface receptors such as CXCR4, which respond to progesterone-induced chemokine gradients, facilitating active homing and targeted migration into the stromal compartment. Progesterone-induced endothelial changes further support stem cell adhesion, rolling, and diapedesis into the tissue. Once engrafted, stem cells secrete growth factors (e.g., HGF, IGF-1, bFGF) that enhance epithelial proliferation, angiogenesis, and stromal repair. In some instances, mesenchymal stem cells may differentiate into endometrial stromal-like cells, replenishing damaged areas. Both progesterone and stem cells both promote a locally anti-inflammatory, pro regenerative environment, reducing fibrosis and allowing structural regeneration (10). Importantly, if stem cells were injected without progesterone priming, the endometrium may remain in a proliferative or atrophic state with lower vascular permeability, less chemokine signaling, and reduced receptivity, impairing stem cell engraftment and therapeutic efficacy. The rationale for evaluation in the mid-secretory phase is because this part of the menstrual cycle represents the most informative time point for clinical evaluation of endometrial receptivity improvements following stem cell therapy. This window allows for the assessment of key surrogate markers, including endometrial thickness, volume, and hysteroscopic scores. These parameters provide measurable evidence of structural and functional regeneration. We understand your concern, which addresses an important methodological aspect in evaluating endometrial histology in patients with intrauterine adhesions (IUA). Geographical heterogeneity of endometrial damage is a well-recognized challenge in Asherman’s Syndrome (AS), and standardizing biopsy site selection is essential to ensure reliable interpretation of histological changes. In this study, as well as in our previous related work (Santamaria X et al., Nature Communications, 2023), biopsy site selection was deliberately standardized. This approach ensured that all samples were collected from bona fide, non-fibrotic endometrium adjacent to the pathological area—tissue most likely to reflect the therapeutic response—while maintaining consistency across timepoints. The posterior wall of the uterine cavity is among the most reproducible and accessible sampling sites, particularly in cases where extensive synechiae may limit access to other regions. Hysteroscopic guidance allowed us to avoid areas of severe fibrosis or necrosis that would preclude meaningful histological evaluation, focusing instead on viable tissue with regenerative potential. Furthermore, the literature acknowledges the existence of different adhesion types (fibrous, muscular, or mixed) that cause variable degrees of damage across the uterine cavity (Foix A et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol, 1966). Our approach accounted for this variability by consistently sampling from the perilesional functional endometrium, which is most relevant for evaluating the impact of cell therapy aimed at tissue regeneration.
